This borrowing bill allows the government to raise money under the Financial Administration Act:
-by way of loan or by the issue and sale of securities of Canada, in such amount or amounts not exceeding in the whole twenty-six billion, four hundred million dollars, as may be required for public works and general purposes.
At the outset, I want to say to the Minister of Finance that when he stated during the 1984 election campaign that it would not be necessary to raise taxes to cut the deficit because all that needs to be done is cut government expenditures, he was laying the groundwork for his own financial management failure.
Since that time, not only has the government cut government services but the Minister of Finance has raised taxes 33 times. The last big tax hike was the GST. What is very discouraging to all Canadians is that in spite of all the cuts and the tax increases, the national debt is still growing by leaps and bounds. Financial management on the part of the government appears to them to be out of control.
Added to this is the longstanding and ongoing concern about the national unity of our country. This does nothing to create confidence in the economy of our nation, and that is sad. It is also sad that we are in the middle of a government created recession.
March 20, 1991

In spite of six years of economic growth which the Minister of Finance himself has called extraordinary, and in spite of 33 separate tax increases to which I have made reference, the accumulated public debt has more than doubled from $166 billion in 1984 to $351 billion in March 1990, and is expected to climb to $389 billion this year. In six years this government has more than doubled the national debt and is well on its way to tripling it. Yet the Minister of Finance back in 1984 thought that this whole matter was so simple that all he had to do was to gain power, get the finance portfolio, cut government expenditures, and the deficit would go away.
That did not happen. Canadians should not bother to listen to what this Minister of Finance has to say about the deficit and the public debt because he has no credibility left on this issue or on any other. The made-in-Canada recession, the Conservative government's first ever made-in-Canada recession, has reduced domestic demand and created an extra burden for our producers here at home.
The Conservative government's monetary policy has caused the dollar to increase from a low of about 69 cents U.S. in February 1986 by 26 per cent to its present level of nearly 87 cents U.S. The Canadian Exporters Association has reported that each cent increase in the exchange rate costs Canada $1.3 billion in lost export sales. That is certainly beginning to tell on the jobs and the unemployment figures across this country.
High interest rates have been used to prop up the Canadian dollar. Although Canadian interests rates have dropped dramatically from a high of over 14.05 per cent on May 24 of last year, they are still about four percentage points higher than the United States rates. This has made the cost of borrowing to modernize or expand prohibitive.
For those in the forest industry, it has had another effect. That famous memorandum of understanding was signed by the present government a few years back on the eve of the signing of the free trade agreement with the United States, whereby Canadian softwood lumber producers were charged a 15 per cent export tax to sell their lumber into the United States. They called it free trade.
Government Orders
Our Canadian manufacturers have had to find other markets and some have gone to Europe. In so doing, after they have sold their product and shipped it, they found that they had to wait for a long time-90 days and even over 100 days in some cases-for their money. As a result, they have to borrow money in order to keep their business floating. They borrow at high interest rates, and this adds to their costs of operation in addition to the 15 per cent that blocked them out of the United States markets. These people are having a very difficult time.
Then there is the old story, all the promises and all the rhetoric about research and development. In spite of Conservative government commitments to raise the level of research and development to 2.5 per cent of the GDP, spending on research and development has declined steadily over the six years of the present government's management, from 1.43 per cent in 1986 to a measly 1.28 per cent of GDP in 1989. The Conservative government has cut funding to the National Research Council by over 20 per cent since 1984-85. Certainly other scientific ventures in this country have been attacked as well.
At a time when the government brags about cutting back and being thrifty, the Fraser Institute, a private non-profit research organization, which monitors government spending and taxation trends, stated in a release on February 18 that "government spending is at an all-time high". The report goes on to say that "spending on defence, police and fire protection across the country are receiving a declining share of the financial pie".
It is very interesting to note that spending on defence, police and fire protection amounts to $835 per capita and has not kept pace with other categories of spending. In fact these functions now get a smaller fraction of total government budgets than they did in 1970.
Cuts in transfer payments to the provinces have meant that provincial funds have had to be redirected in order to make up the shortfall at the provincial level.
Last fall unemployment insurance certainly became a great issue in my area as it did in many others. The bill which was stalled in the Senate for a long time and which was supposed to be such a great boost to all Canadians came into force. In that bill there was a clause that emphasized the benefits to Canadians who are working for relatives, called the arm's length clause. Certainly we can use eastern Ontario as a good example because we have family owned businesses all over the place. When a

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
father laid off his son or brother-in-law or sister-in-law, they then went to apply for unemployment insurance only to find their case had to be passed on to National Revenue for a special ruling to make sure that they were at arm's length from the business.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration says: "That is right". I just wish that minister had been standing in my office when I had some of these people there making representations to me when they had not had a pay cheque for eight or nine weeks and that included Christmas. The government should be ashamed of itself for imposing that kind of restriction on people.
One person had worked for 20 years and had never claimed unemployment insurance. When he went into the office to apply, he ran into this great unemployment insurance rejuvenation bill that was supposed to be such a great boost to him only to find that he had to go through Christmas and New Years and nine weeks without a pay cheque.
There were so many calls over this that the department finally started getting it sorted out. The fact remains it was mismanagement of the legislation. Neither the department of employment nor was the Department of National Revenue was ready for it. Yet we heard screams in the House day after day about how terrible it was that this legislation was being held up. There are many people out there who wish today that it was still being held up.
I have obviously got my message through to the minister today, and I am glad, because many people have suffered through her trying to straighten out her department's relationship with National Revenue and to get the system working. It was not they who straightened it out, it was all those who had complaints and who were having their livelihood taken away from them or denied them.
Mr. Speaker, on the issue of national unity in Canada, which has so much to do with the future direction of our country, in fact almost everything to do with it, I want to share with everyone a very moving experience I had yesterday.
There is a little humorous incident I would like to relate to everybody. While we were in the VIP lounge at Uplands yesterday with the Governor General, the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence, senior military personnel, policy people, and several others, a colonel stepped out and in his usual brisk and efficient manner said that they were going to divide the group into two parties. He said: "We are going to have the red party and we are going to have the blue party". At that stage, the Prime Minister spoke up and said: "Len Hopkins is going to be very lonely out there, we will have to give him a podium all by himself".
The irony of the whole matter is that the Prime Minister ended up in the red party and I was in the blue party. Can you imagine a situation like that for parliamentary unity? There are some great sacrifices one has to make from time to time in this place.
The other thing I want to really zero in on here is the tremendous welcome home for the first field hospital group. They were so glad to hit Canadian soil. You have to witness it to realize what an impact it really has on people. One young man said to me: "Len, I just feel like getting down and kissing the ground". A young nurse said: "You know, in this country we say we live in the greatest country of the world. But you never witness it until you have gone abroad, up to your ankles in mud, unhealthy conditions, see the economy in other certain parts of the world, see the difficulties that people face. You come home and you thank God for your nation".
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you and every member of this House, and all Canadians, will agree that these people are great ambassadors at home for the work they do, but they are fantastic ambassadors when sent abroad. They have done a super job for us.
It presented a real challenge to me yesterday to talk to these people who had gone outside the country, and who had performed their duties so well for Canada, and who delivered the good Canadian message to foreign groups. Here we are at home, in this great nation they love so much, and we have issues here that could split the country wide open.
If there is anything that we, as Canadians, must take from this great experience, it is that we should back off a bit. We should take a look at ourselves in a mirror-and I do not mean just some, I mean everybody-and ask ourselves where we are coming from. Here we do in fact have everything that any human being would want on the face of this earth. God has blessed us with everything that any human being would really want.
March 20, 1991

The Fathers of Confederation put this nation together with great difficulty. Other people have come along since that time and have had tremendous input into it. Many people across this land have come from many other countries and built this nation and developed it. They worked long, hard hours.
I remember, even though I was not very big, the Great Depression of the 1930s. I was not even going to school, but I can remember what people went through at that time. I sometimes look back and wonder how people ever survived that. I think of my mother and father. The thing that I feel brought them through it and helped them to face up to those issues of providing food for their family and remaining very loyal to their country and very interested in their country and managing their affairs very scrupulously was the fact that they had a faith. They had a faith through their own religious beliefs and they practised them.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you have witnessed this yourself, where your own parents taught you many great qualities: humanitarianism, your religious duties, your duty to your country, your duty to do a day's work for a day's pay, and a duty to look toward the future and find out what you can do for mankind.
I can really get carried away on this subject because there is nothing that is more important to every Canadian, from coast to coast and from south to north in this nation today, than to sit down and talk and put this nation together so that it is going to last for generations and centuries to come. It is going to mean a flexibility of our minds. We cannot all be staid in our ways and it is either my way or the highway. That is not the philosophy we are going to have to exercise in this country. It is part of our relationship with our own fellow people.
We as civilians in Canada need the same kind of dedication, breadth of mind, personal discipline, desire and seriousness to keep this country together. We will require a commitment on the part of all Canadians and a flexible attitude on many matters. That is what those young Canadian Forces personnel taught me yesterday. I have been groping for some time to find a real, sincere and open way to express my feelings. I must say, with the words they were expressing yesterday and what they have
Government Orders
come through and their dedication to duty, we must as civilians in this Canadian nation can do our work out there across the country, we must, as 295 members in this House of Commons do our work in a sincere and dedicated manner for this country and open up our minds and communicate well with each other and have a firm commitment. But we must also have faith in ourselves, we must also have faith in our maker and ask for his guidance and we must have faith in our fellow parliamentarians. That is what is going to keep this nation together. I think it would be a great idea if all parties in this House of Commons, perhaps even through you, Mr. Speaker, had a world day of prayer for the Canadian nation, a special service in every church, in every religious centre across the country.
I am delivering this type of speech at this time because we are today passing a bill to borrow billions of dollars to cover the costs of operating the country. We cannot just go on doing this forever. We must work closely together to put things together in this nation and to build the Canadian nation, but we must have that communicating factor and have our total act together.
Those men and women who have returned from the Persian Gulf are expecting parliamentarians in general to work to keep our country strong here at home. If we can do our work here at home as well as they are able to do theirs abroad, we will have it made.
It is important to have a strong federal government in Canada, one that relates in realistic terms to the regions of this country. If Canadians are going to continue to have any of the fine qualities and services of life that have been available to them for many years, this must happen.
There is another angle to this. If Canada is strong at home then we can continue to perform constructively and with humanitarianism in international affairs. When we look back over Canadian history, we have seen many Canadian statesmen who have led the way in many very useful operations in international affairs. Canada has played a role in international affairs far beyond our size and, I suppose, importance as a nation but it has been done. Only if we are strong here at home and have a unified nation in the future, only then can we continue to be a great influence on other nations of the world.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
In order to put this country on a solid footing, accountability on the part of government is extremely important. We had a recent example in this House, and it was raised again today, and I was very much interested in that subject when it was raised in the House today because I had it in my notes to mention it here this afternoon. We had a recent example where the government actually referred the Supplementary Estimates which contained the estimates for the Spicer commission to a parliamentary committee that had not had a chairperson since last September. As you know, this led to a great confrontation in this House.
It also had implications for the public accounts committee, which I have the privilege of chairing because, as you recall, some members in this House wanted to refer the matter to the public accounts committee. That could not happen because I had to reply to a letter that I received requesting this, and I know it was brought to the Prime Minister's attention as well. I must point out that there are serious procedural limitations contained in the mandate of the public accounts committee to carry out such an inquiry in this House at that time. Standing Order 108(3) defines the mandate of the public accounts committees as follows:
The mandate of the Standing Committee on
(e) Public Accounts shall include, among other matters, review of and report on the Public Accounts of Canada and all reports of the Auditor General of Canada, which shall be severally deemed, permanently referred to the Committee immediately they are laid upon the Table;
and any other matter which the House shall from time to time refer to the standing committee.
The term "among other matters" refers to an order of reference from the House of Commons.
The most recent public accounts tabled in October 1990, before the establishment of the Spicer commission, are a comprehensive record of government expenditures for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1990. Expenditures after that date would not be shown in the 1989-90 public accounts and, therefore, we had no estimates from the Spicer commission.
Similarly, the last report of the Auditor General of Canada covers the period ended March 31, 1990. The Spicer commission was brought in after that, so it was not included in that report either.
I regretfully had to say that our existing mandate of the public accounts committee does not permit us to carry out the relevant enquiry. The committee would need an order of reference from this House. However, it is important to note that all commissions of inquiry are accountable to Parliament for the expenditure of public funds. Treasury Board policies govern these expenditures, including the guidance given to all departments and agencies in matters of financial administration by the Office of the Comptroller General.
In addition, financial controls are exercised by the Receiver General's department in the disbursement of moneys. Of course, these expenditures are subject to audit by Parliament's auditor, the Auditor General of Canada.
As members are aware, Supplementary Estimates C, 1990-91, relating to the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future, have been referred to the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations. Because this committee does not have a chairperson, it has not been meeting. Failure to take steps to appoint a chairperson and activate the committee in question will simply indicate a lack of will on the part of Parliament to control the public purse effectively and credibly.
I am glad to see today that Parliament is grappling with that question and I hope it will soon be settled.
The other item I wanted to bring to the attention of the House is a letter that was written to me by the President of the Treasury Board, and it gives me great concern. It does deal very specifically with public accountability.
He said:
In response to the concerns expressed in your previous letter
about the participation of my officials at a meeting that was held on
November 28, and in the future I would like to make my position
clear.
We had requested certain officials to be there to reply and that did not occur. There were officials there, but they were sitting back against the wall.
March 20, 1991

It is my view that officials of the secretariat should, in general, testify as witnesses before the committee in two circumstances.
The rules of this House point out very clearly the powers of committees, and a minister of the Crown should not be telling a parliamentary committee, and particularly the public accounts committee, that on two specific occasions would his officials appear.
The first he said is, and I quote:
-when the Auditor General has specifically directed recommendations or observations to the Treasury Board.
The second is:
-when, in certain instances, it is useful for the committee to have officials of the secretariat available to respond to general questions on specific Teasury Board policies. Beyond these two instances, however, I feel that it is generally inappropriate for secretariat officials to testify as witnesses on matters that relate primarily to the operations of other departments.
The problem here is that Treasury Board is supposed to be the controller of the purse, and lays down guidelines for government departments and their expenditures.
We have taken it, and it has been a tradition, that officials from Treasury Board can appear when the Auditor General is there or appear when people are there from other departments.
Going on with the minister's letter, he says:
The accountability of other departments to the Public Accounts committee would not, in my view, ordinarily be served by such participation. These criteria govern the arrangements that were explicitly made with members of your staff regarding participation of the secretariat at the committee meeting of November 28, 1990 which was addressing the project to modernize the CCGS Louis Saint-Laurent, the icebreaker.
There are differences of opinion on that discussion as well. He goes on:
Pursuant to discussions with senior officials of the secretariat, your staff agreed that my officials would only observe at the meeting.
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that that was not my understanding at all.
It was also agreed that any issues raised by the committee touching on the role of Treasury Board would be promptly followed up on thereafter.
With regard to "thereafter", the purpose of holding committee meetings, particularly those on accountability, of an accountability role, is to have these people there to answer questions, and put those answers on the
Government Orders
records of the committee meeting at the time. A person who was there did not come up to the table at the time when we asked for a person from Treasury Board. Another person did, but apparently nobody was really designated to do it.
The minister went on to say:
With respect to the meeting of your committee on December 18, 1990 on the subject of the Louis Saint-Laurent icebreaker, please be advised that either Mr. David McEachran, deputy secretary of the Administrative Policy Branch, or Mr. Richard Paton, Assistant Secretary in the same branch, will be attending in order to respond to questions of the committee on Teasury Board's policies touching on the management of projects.
They came to that meeting. There is no sense in senior officials advising ministers that they do not have a role to play at committee meetings in the House of Commons. I totally disagree with the suggestion that Treasury Board should not be present at meetings when they are asked to be there in relation to other departments. I want to make that very clear.
It is spelled out clearly in Beauchesne that a parliamentary committee can send for persons, papers, et cetera, and can invite people to appear before the committee. If those people do not want to attend, the committee can order them to attend. You are well aware of that, Mr. Speaker.
I want to send a message to senior people in Treasury Board that they, too, are accountable to the Parliament of Canada.
I hope that Parliament will come to grips with picking a chairman for the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations so that that issue can be heard and decided upon.
I want to touch briefly on Public Service 2000, which is a very important part of government policy in the management of its employees. Our public accounts committee recommended that a special committee be set up to hear the Public Service 2000 issues. We felt that this would have to be an in-depth study. We certainly did not have time to do it, even though it was in the Auditor General's report. We had about six meetings on it and we submitted our report to the House. The President of the Treasury Board said that he would like to have a special committee study Public Service 2000. He also went on to say that he was going to consult with other people in the Public Service and with unions.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
There was a time at a news conference when I was a bit concerned because the President of Treasury Board had indicated that there was no agreement for a special committee on this, and he blamed my own House leader at the time as one who did not agree with it. That was certainly not true. Our own House leader did agree with it.
I hope that the President of Treasury Board will continue to agree, as he did in a recent letter to me a second time, saying that he will refer the matter for a special hearing. There are certain things about which Treasury Board has the full right, as the government of the day, to make regulations. However, as we continue here, we should have some in-depth hearings on this because these people are the backbone of government in doing the work and providing a service to Canadians.
Budget matters are closely related to the bill before us today because the borrowing bill supplements what the budget does not provide for. There are many things here that are really very important to Canadians. Again, it is a matter of getting our house in order.
The government of the day is simply passing the responsibility for a larger share of medicare and post-secondary education over to the provinces. This is coming right down to the municipal level in the provinces because the provinces have to transfer more money into providing these other services and they have fewer grants to offer to municipalities. Therefore, the addition has to be made up in the taxation of the local municipality.
The government now admits that it will need amendments to the Canada Health Act to protect Canadians. It will have to use a big stick in the provinces, forcing them to provide proper services to Canadians because the federal government is refusing to give the provinces the cash.
Then we go on to unemployment, where the Minister of Finance in his budget predicted greater unemployment. We are certainly seeing it across the country and we are certainly seeing it in my own region of eastern Ontario.
We forecast that the government would have to raise unemployment insurance premiums to cover the cost of unemployment insurance changes contained in Bill C-21.
The government promised gradual increases. Its interpretation of gradual increases was the 24 per cent increase that it brought in, in the budget, to cover UIC changes. That has hurt small business and it is certainly taken from the people's paycheques.
Training and education have both been hit by the budget. A new study on transfer payments is supposed to come out this spring. I have said before, and I will say it again, that the day is not far off when there will have to be a royal commission once again into the study of the dividing up of the financial pie in this country between the federal government and the provinces. Otherwise, the whole thing is going to be out of whack again.
I am talking about a commission similar to the Rowell-Sirois commission of 1937, which has served us well over the years but which is now being torn apart.
Regional development was not really mentioned. It is going to come later, and we can expect that it will be all bad news. In eastern Ontario we have lost VIA Rail service from Ottawa to North Bay. The forest industry is down. Large numbers have been laid off in that industry. Agriculture is certainly not witnessing very pleasant days in many respects. Industries have closed. Nobody seems to be listening. We do not have any regional development plans for eastern Ontario.
I do not want to burden the Minister of Employment and Immigration any more. I hate to see her disturbed because she is such a nice individual to talk to. She is approachable as a minister, but I know she has been rather upset by some of my comments on that terrible UI legislation.
I want to close by making a tribute to the Auditor General of Canada. I can well recall some of the governments which I supported over the years; we did not always like what the Auditor General said. This government is no different. As parliamentarians, and the Auditor General being a servant of Parliament, there is not a member of the House who should not support the Office of the Auditor General very firmly.
I think Kenneth Dye has served this nation well. I have had the privilege of working very closely with him over the last two years plus, as have other members of the committee. We have found him to be very candid, open, up-front and well informed on his subjects.
March 20, 1991

He comes out with his reports and we see in this House where they become a great foofaraw for a couple of days. Then it dies down, and it is left to the public accounts committee to do the work for days thereafter. It is a pleasure to do that. We who serve on the public accounts committee have enjoyed it. It is a very broad perspective on government.
Kenneth Dye is a dedicated man. He has done his utmost to serve Canadians and this Parliament well. He is also served well by a very capable staff, people who are in place to do a job for him, to do his research. Also, in his important role to Canadians, he is seen as the defender of the purse.
I said to him the other day that during his term in office he learned the approach of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, when Franklin Delano Roosevelt used to have his little fireside chats. He would turn on the American nation, get them over to his side, and then Congress would have to vote along with him or the pressure came from the American public. We have known Kenneth Dye to be an outspoken person who had no hesitation to raise issues publicly. When the Canadian people heard him speak, they respected him and brought that to the attention of parliamentarians. This is an office, Mr. Speaker, that reports to Parliament through you. The Auditor General is a servant of Parliament. We thank Ken Dye and his people for the service they have provided to the House, to the Parliament of Canada in general and to the people of Canada.
We wish our new Auditor General every success. It is not an easy job dealing with politicians from time to time, but they all come into it knowing full well what their role is. I hope the new Auditor General will have the support of this House as he takes on his new duties.
There are other things about which I would like to speak, but I am going to stop here because I am sure there are other people who want to comment. Besides that, I am losing my voice, so it may not be by voluntary consent. I want to thank you for your time, Mr. Speaker, and I want to thank the members of the House for their patience.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:

We will now proceed to the next speaker who will have 20 minutes plus 10 minutes of questions and comments.

Mr. Speakers, I have first to congratulate my predecessor on a marathon session which has covered a great deal of ground. As usual he has made some very important points reflecting his experience in the public accounts committee.
We have in front of us a very large amount of money which this government is asking this Parliament to grant it. This bill, if it passes the House, will authorize the government of this country to borrow as much as $26.4 billion.
That is such a large amount of money that it is almost inconceivable to the average person in this country. It is not the kind of thing which is easy to think about. If we think of it in terms of this country of 26 million, each of us is permitting the government to borrow $1,000 on our behalf. Each and every person across this country is giving authorization to this government to borrow $1,000.
We have to ask the question: Is this a government which has earned the right to do that kind of massive borrowing on behalf of the people of Canada? Since it came before Parliament and last asked for authority to borrow from the people of Canada, does its record in the past year show a sensitivity to the concerns of the people of Canada? Does its record show that it has financially organized its affairs well? Does its record show that its economic leadership in particular gives reason for confidence to those 26 million Canadians?
Absolutely.

The minister says: "Absolutely". I have to say absolutely not.
I am sure when the minister has had a chance to work her way through the large amounts of correspondence with which she has to deal and looks at some of the fresh statistics which have emerged today, she will realize how devastating they are with respect to this government's record. I am sure that she cannot be pleased to see that the number of bankruptcies in this country are up by 68

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
per cent in the past year. Bankruptcies, especially in the province of Ontario, are more than double what they were.
There is an NDP government there.

She mentions that there is an NDP government there. The reason for that is that the Liberal government in Ontario, as well as this government, did such a poor job that on September 6, 1990 it was swept out of power, just as this government will be hopefully swept out of power in the very near future. I hope the minister survives because the minister is somebody I look forward to facing when she is in opposition.
A total of 430,000 jobs have been lost in this country in the last year. This government used to boast about how it would have created 200,000 jobs a year. I think at one stage it even got up to 300,000 jobs a year. Whereas in one year it has lost 430,000 permanent jobs. That comes directly out of Statistics Canada's own figures, in case the minister is searching for the source.
The impact has been especially difficult in the manufacturing sector. Employment in manufacturing has declined by 11.7 per cent in the past year. That means that out of every 10 jobs in manufacturing a year ago, 1.2 of those jobs has disappeared. Can you conceive that there has been such a destruction of jobs in manufacturing, Mr. Speaker? If you think that is bad, you just have to look at construction where the result has been a decrease of 12.1 per cent in the past year.
Part-time employment, it is true, has increased. Parttime employment has gone up by 98,000. That is not because people want part-time jobs. It is because that is all they can get. However, 430,000 of those permanent jobs that they would prefer have disappeared.
It is not just bankruptcy statistics and unemployment statistics. It is the international trade statistics that came out today that we should also look at. What the government said to us was that we in this country were going to thrive because of free trade. Free trade was going to be the solution. The minister's business friends went across the country spending millions of dollars to buy the last election for this government on the promise that there would be hundreds of thousands of new jobs thanks to trade.
What has happened? Let's look at the statistics.
The statistics tell us that for January exports actually decreased by $352 million and that instead of imports decreasing too, imports increased by $244 million.
That means in fact that the surplus which existed in January of this year was just $166 million. That compares with a surplus of a billion dollars in the month previous. In fact, if we look at the trend, it has been downward in that surplus. Instead of the free trade deal giving us benefits, it has been costing us exports and leading to new imports into this country.
That is why we see the jobs disappearing across Canada. That is why the 430,000 jobs that have been lost, disappeared in this last year. Of course it has to do with things like the high interest rates this government has followed. It has to do with the fact that the value of the Canadian dollar, which they have kept, is far too high.
A former cabinet minister from this government suggested that this was part of the free trade deal arrangement, that the dollar had to be kept high, to keep the United States interested in signing the free trade deal. The 430,000 jobs lost as a result of that high dollar and the high interest rates are probably related to the free trade deal too.
I can tell you that in my constituency, and in the constituencies of many of the people that are around me today in the House, there has been a devastating loss of jobs directly, because of free trade.
In my constituency, 40 plants shut last year, 40 factories that were providing work with people. In many cases they not only shut down, they transferred their operations to the United States or to Mexico. The government, with its immense wisdom, looking at this trend, has decided to make it even easier for companies to transfer to Mexico. Instead of trying to do something about the loss of jobs and the loss of factories, they have entered into trade negotiations with Mexico, to try to make it possible to shift even more jobs to the low wage parts of Mexico. Sheer insanity.
If this was just a set of statistics, if it was just a set of bad numbers, if it was just something one could point to as signs that the government had not given us what it promised, that would be one thing. What we have seen is terrible, terrible human consequences across this country as a result of what has taken place. These consequences are obvious when you talk about hundreds of thousands of jobs being lost.
March 20, 1991

What is even worse is that many of those people who in the past would have been able to get unemployment insurance so that they could support themselves and help the rest of the economy through the support they were getting, have as a result of this government's deliberate policy been cut off unemployment insurance.
The consequence has been contrary to anything that the minister of employment ever predicted would happen. We have thousands and thousands of people, in her own home city, who are having to go on welfare; skilled workers, people who are anxious to find training, people who go to unemployment insurance offices and ask for training. They ask for the chance to be part of training programs, and you know what they are told, Mr. Speaker?
You're on your own.
They are told: "Well, we'll put your name on the list, but we have a two-year waiting list".
That is because you held up the legislation.

They are told that there is a massive waiting list. They are told that this government which promised people training has instead cut $100 million from the Canadian Jobs Strategy.
For instance, if they happen to be refugees they are told-as a group who spoke with us on Monday night, the Ontario Coalition of Agencies Serving Immigrants, a group which later met with the minister's department- that there simply is not enough money.
Every time the minister comes back into the House she gets straightened out. I am sorry about that.
The reality is that her extra money which she talks about for language training has led to groups telling us on Monday night, for instance groups from her own home city, who are part of this Ontario Coalition of Agencies Serving Immigrants, that they had only 75 places to be able to offer and over 3,000 people were asking for the chance to get help, for the chance to have an ability to learn languages, to be able to work in this countiy. I am sorry she has been scared out again.
Government Orders
The reality is, as somebody from Peel told us, that they have pages of waiting lists of people who need help and who are not able to get that help.
The reality is that people across this country are being severely damaged. Refugees, of course, but also millions of Canadian families who have seen people within their family face unemployment, have not been able to get unemployment insurance and have had to go on welfare. They have seen their dignity, their pride in their ability to provide for their families destroyed.
What does this government do in its budget, having cut back unemployment insurance already? It takes the next step and it cuts back its support to welfare payments.
This is a shameful government. It is a government which has shown on issue after issue, case after case, that it does not care about people. It has shown that it is incompetent as well.
But cares about some people.

As my colleague from Edmonton suggests, it cares about those people to whom it extended the 21-year trust agreements. It did not have to do that, but for those large family foundations, those family fortunes which were tied up in trust, that were supposed to run out this year, yes it had something for them. It has had something for the large corporations that wanted to maintain their memberships in golf courses and their special boxes in the Sky Dome, and their special boxes for Edmonton Oilers games. Oh yes, it permitted

And also for the Quebec Nordiques!
It permitted those companies to continue to deduct 80 per cent of the cost of those entertainment expenditures from the taxes that people across this country pay. It ends up, Mr. Speaker, and I know you feel as strongly about this as I do, that you and I and the 26 million Canadians across this country have to pay more taxes to support these freebies for corporate executives and their friends who get to go to sporting events.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
Now you and I, Mr. Speaker, both like to go to sporting events, but we are prepared to pay the cost, as people across this country pay the cost, unless the giant corporations in this country get the chance to buy in to special privileges and deduct it from taxes that you and I have to make up.
Lest you think that this is just a New Democrat raving in the wilderness, let me quote from another judgment on the budget from the Toronto Dominion Bank. I think you would agree-even the minister of defence would agree-the Toronto Dominion Bank is not usually an ally of the New Democratic Party.
The Toronto Dominion Bank is a friend of the socialists.

See, he agrees, it is not usually an ally of the New Democratic Party. Therefore, let me quote from the Toronto Dominion Bank's analysis of this budget. I could quote a great deal from this, but let me just quote perhaps the most devastating comment: "This 1991 budget is probably the most economically inept and destructive budget since the 1930s." That is not us speaking, that is the Toronto Dominion Bank.
What we have got is a set of judgments from across the country from the people whom we represent that tell us this government has lost its compassion, if indeed it ever had it. It has lost its ability to listen to Canadians. It has lost its ability to care about Canadians and, most important, it has lost its ability to lead Canadians. Canadians no longer trust this government. That is why we will be voting against letting this government borrow over $26 billion from the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I was listening to the hon. member of the NDP, who said earlier that members on this side of the House work only for Canadians who are well off. Perhaps I may comment and I will also have a question a little later on that I have three riding offices. In those offices, I have assistants who are working with me on cases involving disabled persons. We even work on cases involving the province, unemployment cases, welfare cases, cases of economic hardship, and we certainly do not work exclusively for families that are well off. We also work for the middle class, including miners.
He referred earlier to freebies for big corporations. Perhaps we should also talk about isolated post allowances for people who live in Abitibi and in northern Quebec, and I am referring to the designation of isolated posts for the purposes of Northern benefits, something we have finally been able to obtain for our workers, our union members, miners, forestry workers and nurses. Everybody-low-income people, the middle class and the upper class-will be on the same footing. They will all get these isolation allowances from the federal government. This is important in the north and in Lebel-sur-Quevillon, Matagami and Joutel. The same applies to Chapais and Chibougamau. In Chibougamau, they were never able to get these allowances but they are now getting 50 per cent. This is wonderful, and we won thanks to the work done by ministers like Benoit Bouchard who represents the riding of Roberval an excellent minister.
I also have a question for the hon. member. He often refers to newspaper articles. In today's papers, Mr. Speaker, and more specifically in La Presse, on the business page there is a reference to something he didn't mention in his speech, and I am talking about mortgage rates. He didn't mention those at all. However, it's all here in the papers. But I know why he didn't mention this, because when he read the papers this morning, while he was having breakfast, he must have felt he couldn't mention this in his speech because the news was much too good.
I have here an article by Nicole France Bernier which says: "Outlook for mortgage customers brighter than in 1982. The number of people in arrears on their residential mortgages has increased substantially over the past few months, but the situation is certainly not alarming, according to financial institutions contacted by La Presse. In fact, it compares favourably with the situation during the last recession". The article goes on to say, Mr. Speaker: "At the Confederation des caisses populates et d'economie Desjardins, which has about 40 per cent of the residential mortgage market in Quebec, Mr. Gaston Sirois, vice-president, financial credit, said that in his opinion, the recession in the early 80s had been much harder on residential mortgage holders, because interest rates were much higher, which made things much harder for people who had to renew their mortgages."
March 20, 1991

So I would like to say to the hon. member that the situation is better than in Ontario, because in September 1981, mortgage rates were as high 21.5 per cent, compared with 11.5 or 11.75 per cent today.
My question is: Why didn't he mention mortgage rates in his speech?

Mr. Speaker, it is not for me to say that Conservatives and Liberals are different. It is not for me to say that the Conservatives kept interest rates lower than the Liberals did during the previous recession. That may be true, but the important question for ordinary people, for all Quebeckers, is this: With the Conservatives or the Liberals can we expect to have an economic policy which would be a promising approach for ordinary people?
I for one cannot see that. I see very high interest rates with the Conservatives, and I saw very high interest rates with the Liberals. I saw the Conservatives offer a number of tax concessions to the major corporations, just as I saw the Liberals do the same thing. There is no difference. Here is the important message getting through to the people of Quebec, to the voters of Quebec. The important message is that there is another choice, there is an alternative, and that is the NDP which can change the situation for a good many Quebeckers. That is reality.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in this debate on such an important piece of legislation affecting the Canadian economy.
Last February when the Minister of Finance presented his sixth budget, we in the Official Opposition said that it was a blueprint for a made-in-Canada recession.
As I rise to address the House today, we have a made-in-Canada recession and the blame for it lies squarely on the doorstep of the Minister of Finance and his boss, the Prime Minister of Canada.
We told the government and members of Parliament on that side, if they continued with their high interest rate, high dollar policy that thousands of Canadians would go bankrupt and hundreds of thousands would lose their jobs.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
Just today, the statistics for the month of February were released and we find that bankruptcies have increased significantly in this country, particularly in the province of Ontario, and we are seeing thousands upon thousands of Canadians losing their jobs on a monthly and regular basis.
We told the government of the Prime Minister that if it insisted on cutting payments to the provinces for things like health care and higher education, it would lead to cutbacks in service, higher tuition fees and higher provincial taxes. This has come to pass. We told the government at that time if it went ahead with the GST, it would push an economy on the brink of recession into full recession and add dangerously to inflation. It too, came to pass. But the government would not listen. It would not listen to the concerns of the opposition and, more important, it would not listen to the concerns of Canadians from coast to coast. It would not listen to the unemployed, to people struggling to pay their rent and to meet the mortgage. They are victims of its terrible, terrible economic planning. It would not listen to leading economists and business people, all of whom warned the government that it was on an economic collision course. The government, much to my chagrin and I am sure to that of many Canadians, still is not listening with regard to the Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if you know that the Minister of Finance did not even have the common decency to stay in the House of Commons to listen to the budget response of the Liberal finance critic, the hon. member from Windsor. In fact, there was only one government minister in the House, the Minister of unemployment and immigration and she was so wrapped up in what she was reading that she didn't seem to hear a word of what our finance critic was saying on behalf of thousands of Canadians across this country.
We now have an economy in serious recession. Unemployment is at 10.2 per cent nationally-and I want to come back to that, Mr. Speaker-10.2 per cent nationally. It is more than 11 per cent in Nova Scotia, and in my constituency in the Cape Breton region, it is a shameful 18.5 per cent.
The figures in parts of Newfoundland are equally high. Parts of northern Ontario and other communities throughout the country, even in the city of Montreal, unemployment is at a shameful high.
It all adds up to close to a million and a half unemployed people in this country, every one of them a tragedy in economic terms and, more important, in human terms.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is there anything in this budget for those people that would help them find jobs or learn the skills necessary for good jobs?
The answer, unfortunately, is no.
All the government has done for the unemployed in this country is to take off $100 million under the Canada Jobs Strategy program. All the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister, and of course his senior political minister in my province of Nova Scotia are saying to the unemployed, those thousands of individuals in my small province, is that "you're on your own; the federal government will not be there to assist you in any way".
In this very budget the Minister of Finance is predicting double digit unemployment right across the country for the rest of this year. He is predicting not much better for the year following, 9.8 per cent right across this country. Shameful predictions, and I think it indicates quite clearly that the government and this Minister of Finance and this Prime Minister have lost control of the economic agenda in this country.
What he is saying is, in effect: "We don't care what the cost is in economic and human terms. Stay the course and, before you know it, this cut and slash approach will lead us out of the recession". Ha, ha, ha; that is what Canadians say to the Minister of Finance. Or, better still; shame, shame, shame on the Minister of Finance of this country.
I see the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader has entered the House. He knows only too well, coming from a province like Alberta, that they understand, particularly in his riding, what it means to be unemployed. I am sure that he shares with me wholeheartedly my sentiments as expressed toward the Minister of Finance.
Canadians have good reason to be sceptical about this government. Last year the Minister of Finance told Canadians that after a bit of a slow period in the spring and summer of 1990, we will be into a mini-boom by the fall. That is what he said-Ripley's "believe it or not".
March 20,1991

When his economic policies drove the country into a real recession, he was the last to admit it. No matter how hard he tried, he just could not get that "r" word, "recession", to roll off his tongue.
His boss, the right hon. Prime Minister, had an easier time. Not only did he acknowledge that the economy was going down the drain, he, in this House and outside the House, had the unmitigated gall to try to take credit for it.
When asked last October about the recession, the Prime Minister said:
We have induced a slowdown. Mr. Wilson said as much in his last
budget. Look at the budget. It is as clear as spring water. Mr. Wilson
spelled it out.
That is what the Prime Minister said, and he and the Minister of Finance took credit for inducing the first ever made-in-Canada recession. I say again through you, Sir, that that is shameful behaviour coming from the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister of this country.
If the Prime Minister wishes to take credit for this made-in-Canada recession, he must also take credit for inducing a million and a half Canadians out of their jobs. That is no laughing matter. That is a serious indictment against any government and against any Minister of Finance. Now we are in a recession and the government has taken credit for it. What is it going to do? What are the ministers going to do to try to get us out of this recession? I wonder what the Minister of National Defence, who is in the Chamber, would do if he were the Minister of Finance. Does he have a plan? No, there is no meaningful plan.
When you pick up the plan for economic recovery, there is nothing in it. It is the government's so-called plan for economic recovery, over nine pages long and not even full-size pages at that. That is all that the thousands and thousands of economists, statisticians and analysts working for the Minister of Finance could come up with for the million and a half unemployed people in this country. I would have thought that the Minister of Finance, who is from one of the wealthiest areas in the country, could have found within his budget a small sum of money to enter into a contract with numerous consultants to come up with some better economic plan than nine short pages for the million and a half Canadians that are unemployed because of this government's first ever made-in-Canada recession.
Government Orders
The Minister of Finance ought to be, must be, ashamed of himself and of the policies that he has been putting forward for quite some time.
We know it is not in the budget. There is no meaningful and complete plan to get us out of the recession created by the Minister of Finance. There is nothing to help the unemployed. The victims of the government's made-in-Canada recession accept the $100 million cut, as members on this side have alluded to on numerous occasions. But what is in the budget? The Minister of Finance would say that there are no new income taxes in the budget. That is what he said in response to my colleague, the deputy leader, the hon. member for Hamilton East, and to the finance critic for our party.
What he will not admit, Mr. Speaker-and I know you find this somewhat misleading; I would not want to say that it is unparliamentary-is that there are things in the budget that will be quite taxing to people's incomes, like the 25 per cent increase in unemployment insurance premiums.
Let's picture for a moment the Minister of Finance saying "no new taxes". A small businessperson running a small store, a retail outlet, a small manufacturing plant, a consulting business, now has to pay higher premiums for the unemployment that he will give to those individuals that he will have to lay off because of the minister's made-in-Canada recession, which he took credit for. The employees will also pay higher premiums for the unemployment insurance that they will get eventually because of lay-off notices.
That is going to take a bite out of the pay cheque of every working man and woman in this country. The Minister of Finance will not come clean with Canadians and call it a tax.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: He does not care.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
That is right. A colleague of mine has referred to the fact that he does not care. I think that is a very appropriate statement with regard to the Minister of Finance.
Do not forget either that this is the same minister who, in 1985, hit Canadians with an income tax surtax which he said was only temporary. In 1986, he made it permanent, and in 1989 he increased it from 3 per cent to 5 per cent on the income of every working person in this country. He does not talk about these income taxes in his budget, even though they are still going on. No new taxes. What do you call that? There is also a three cent per cigarette tax. At least the minister is honest about that particular tax.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
The most staggering tax in Canadian history, the GST, just took effect this past January. I suggest to my colleague from Newfoundland, that the Minister of Finance would have to be deaf, dumb, and blind, to suggest that this has not hit hard on the pocket-books of Canadians. It is absolutely, unequivocally ridiculous for the Minister of Finance to allude that the GST is not a tax and it is not part of his particular budget. Does he say that in the budget? Of course not. What does he say about the GST? I will tell you. Here is what he says: "The Prime Minister has given a commitment that any above-projected revenues from the GST will make a contribution to deficit reduction".
The Minister of Finance wants to use the GST to reduce the deficit. This is about the most cynical thing I have seen from this government in recent time.
The GST and the implications that it has for average Canadians is absolutely devastating. The member opposite is shaking his head in agreement. I know that the hon. member is an honourable individual. I know it was difficult for him to vote in favour of this government's policies. And I know that if the occasion were to arise again, he would want to stand in his place and say to his colleagues in the government: "Scrap the GST, let us move on to real tax reform; let us not aggravate and exacerbate this first ever made-in-Canada recession by the Minister of Finance".
The Minister of Finance in implementing this particular tax led us to believe it was going to be revenue neutral. Well, that is supposed to mean that when you bring in a so-called replacement tax, it will not bring in any more money for the government than the tax is supposed to replace.
We in the Official Opposition said all along that the GST was much more than just a replacement tax. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for this opportunity to take part in this important debate. It is a very clear message emanating from the Budget which the Conservative government tabled a few weeks ago. It is definitely a disaster for ordinary Canadians. How not to reach this conclusion, when we realize that this Budget will seriously damage the social fabric of our country with its tax increases and spending cuts.
Clearly, Canadians will wonder what they did to deserve such a government. The economic situation now is far from brilliant: 1.5 million Canadians are unemployed because of the government's economic policies. Last year, the number of bankrupticies reached 55,000. One out of every six Canadian children goes to bed every night on an empty stomach.
When faced with such a serious situation, what does the government do? Well, Mr. Speaker, I am going to tell you. It shirks its commitments. Not only is it responsible for the economic mess everywhere in this country, but its policies are only making a bad situation worse. As a matter of fact, the government has withdrawn nearly $1 billion from its programs for the needy and increased by 24 per cent the unemployment insurance premiums and this, right in the middle of an economic recession.
For that matter, Canadians were looking forward to a Budget which would ease to a certain extent the devastating impact of the recession and would help promote national unity. Unfortunately, they were offered a Budget which slashes in the job creation programs, attacks health care, education and the unions, and continues the Prime Minister's policy which is to transfer to the provinces the burden of its federal deficit.
What is really unbelievable about the deficit is that the Tories have the gall to tell Canadians they must tighten their collective belt to reduce it.
Whoever looks at table 3 on page 91 of the document entitled "the Budget", published by the Minister of Finance, realizes that the government is playing an interesting little game. The government has increased personal income tax by 8.7 per cent, while reducing corporate income tax by 3.5 per cent.
Moreover, according to the government's budgetary document, personal income tax will have increased by 22.5 per cent in the fiscal year 1990-91 and 1991-92,
Government Orders
while corporate income tax will have decreased by 15.9 per cent. It is unbelievable!
On the basis of these facts, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the government is not really serious about debt and deficit reduction. In fact, since coming to power in 1984, it has more than doubled the national debt.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the Tory government is only using the debt as an excuse for slashing social programs.
[English)
The aim of this government is to dismantle Canada's social programs by cutting back in transfer payments to which the provinces have a constitutional right. It is in the Constitution that the Government of Canada has to help out with regional disparities and has to try to equalize. It is those very equalization payments that the government is cutting back. It is cutting back on payments that will serve to go toward health care and post-secondary education.
In the projections of this government from 1986 to 1996 it expects to cut $40 billion on these transfer payments to the provinces. In my province of New Brunswick alone, it expects to cut over a billion dollars in these transfer payments. These transfer payments are for education. They are for health care. Certainly this is a direct attack on medicare.
Speaking of medicare, last evening we had occasion to witness the government in full bloom, so to speak. We had a motion in the House concerning medicare and saying that this House now supports medicare, wants to support it, and wants to continue it. We know how that vote came about and what the results were. Again it is a demonstration that this government has no commitment to medicare. It is a direct attack on medicare. It is just a matter of time with the cuts to these transfer payments that medicare will be a thing of the past.
Looking at the money that this government wants to borrow to institute its budgetary plan, we must look at the state of the economy and see what part of the economy is suffering and what type of plan this government is putting in place to help these people who are suffering.
There are, as I mentioned previously, a million and a half people out of work. The projections the finance minister has given us so far have stated they are going to be in double-digit numbers for the next year or so, and he has accepted that. It is one thing to accept it, but it is another thing not to do anything about it.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
The high unemployment rate is a direct link, a direct cause, to the high interest rate and high dollar policies of this government. There is no doubt about it. It has cost businesses jobs. It has cost industry jobs. There is no doubt about it. There is a direct link.
As many members mentioned today on the same topic, the high interest rate and high dollar policy has affected our export ability and has created this first made-in-Ca-nada recession.
What has the government done to help the unemployed? If we look at the budget documents, we find that in the Canadian Jobs Strategy, the area where it is supposed to be helping the unemployed, it has cut $100 million.
If we tiy to figure out what that will mean to each province, we would have to play a guessing game based on past traditions. In New Brunswick alone, this would mean a cutback of $6.5 million. As you know, Mr. Speaker, there are many places in New Brunswick that suffer from high unemployment.
I come from such a region, and I want to point out some of the figures that exist in my region. In February, the unemployment rate in my riding was 16.3 per cent. The average rate for Canada in February was 10.2 per cent. What has the minister done? He has cut these programs to help these people get back to work.

Mr. Speaker, there is no relief for the fishermen in my riding. There is no relief for the farmers in my riding. There is no relief for the workers in the mining and forest industries in my riding.

I have to say it is not getting much better. I do not want to seem a pessimist, because I am noted for being a person who likes to move ahead and talk about positive things.
Just this week alone, I received a call giving me some very sad information. Two major industries in my riding; one, a kraft mill-we know what type of employment it has-has been put up for sale because of poor markets and because it is not competitive. It exports, and we
know what the high dollar has done to exports. Hopefully a buyer will be found and the mill will continue.
Even sadder, in Kedgwick which is a small community with very high unemployment, the sawmill is up for sale and must be sold by the end of June. If not, the present owner plans on closing. The unemployment rate in that area is probably much higher than most other areas in my riding, well above 20 per cent. That impacts on about 100 full-time jobs and well over 200 seasonal jobs. It is a small community of roughly 2,500 people.
I may as well make the pitch now and hope that the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Minister of Labour will look upon this area as a special area, that they will try to apply some of the adjustment programs that now exist into this area and that they will use a little more flexibility.
Speaking about flexibility, I should also say that my region has been hit by a number of strikes in the past year. One is still ongoing from July 1990 where approximately 1,500 employees have been out on strike. I have written to the minister asking for more flexibility in applying UIC regulations. I would again hope that for the sake of the families of men, women and children involved, with the suffering that they are going through that the government would show more flexibility in that regard. I would also hope that the government would try to convince both sides to get back to the bargaining table and resolve those labour disputes as quickly as possible without, rightly so, interfering in the process. I know it is private sector.
I would also like to talk a little bit about income tax because the government is saying there have been no increases in taxes. The government is telling us how it has closed loopholes on corporations. I want to refer to this government document entitled "The Budget". I think many of us are familiar with it. On page 91 of the budget, Table 3 sets out budgetary revenues. I guess the government needs money to operate and that is what we are debating tonight. We are looking at where that money is going. When we look at where it is getting that money from, there is a table on page 91 that is very interesting. It is a breakdown of where it gets its money in relation to personal income and corporate income.
March 20,1991

We find on that table that in 1990-91, the government would be getting 13.8 per cent more revenue from personal income than the year before. This is an increase. It is getting more revenue from individuals. If you look at the same table for corporate income tax you will see a decrease of 12.4 per cent from 1990 to 1991. What this table is telling us is that individuals are paying more and corporations are paying less.
If we look at the table a little further and in more depth, we will find that from 1991 to 1992, which are only projections but the minister lives by those projections, we will find that the individual personal income tax revenue for the government will increase by 8.7 per cent and the corporate income tax will decrease by 3.5 per cent. If you add up the totals for both years, you will find that the revenue from income tax for individuals will be increased to 23.7 per cent while, in fact, for the corporations it will decrease to 15.6 per cent. Again, individuals are paying more and corporations are paying less. I think it is veiy important that that point was made this evening.
In conclusion, because I know my time is limited and I do not want to go on too long, I just want to make the point that the government seems to have, as my hon. House leader mentioned a while ago, more or less embarked on a policy of telling Canadians: "You are on your own". We have talked about transfer payments, medicare: "You are on your own, provinces." We talk about post-secondary education for students: "You are on your own."
I was speaking to a student just the other day who was at the ceremony for Rev. Sean O'Sullivan, and I asked him when he was home last. He was from Cape Breton and a former page of the House. He said it had been quite some time. I said: "You did not go home last summer?" He said: "No, I didn't. There was no work back home, unfortunately." He said: "I had to work all summer. I am working now part-time. You know, even with all that work, I still do not have enough money to pay for my post-secondary education."
It is getting worse. There is a tax on the administration of student loans now. What is coming to is that post-secondary education is going to be for the rich, unfortunately, very unfortunately.
Government Orders
This budget and this bill are both linked. Bill C-97 is linked to the budget because it will provide the money for the budget to operate. This is a disastrous budget; it is simply disastrous. It is an attack on the regions, it is an attack on the poor, it is an attack on students, it is an attack on national unity. You may ask, why national unity? We all know the crisis situation that Canada is in, we know that when people are unhappy they like to look at other options. So it is quite obvious what this budget has done.
It is an attack on rural Canada, it is an attack on the fabric of Canada, it is an attack on medicare. I would hope that the government would come back to a compassionate type of system, a system which I think is necessary to solve and to resolve the problems that Canadians are being faced with, not only on a national level but on a regional level as well.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
I ask my colleague whether he believes that these policies of the government have been addressed in any way in the budgetary programs of the Minister of Finance, and whether he believes, as I believe, that rural revitalization ought to be a major component of any economic plan that any government would put before the people of Canada.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. House leader for the question.
I think, in all honesty, if we were to look at what has happened to rural Canada in the last number of years, we will find that, yes, the budget does address rural Canada, but in a negative way unfortunately.
I don't know whether there is a misunderstanding in cabinet, in government, but it claims that: "Oh, we have the programs, if you can't find a job in rural Canada we are going to move you, you can apply for a little grant and we will move you and you can find a job in Toronto or in Montreal". Well, we know what has happened in Montreal and we know what is going to happen in Toronto and Vancouver.
Its little plan is to take rural Canada and practically dismantle it. That is quite obvious. It is a plan that has been there all along.
We look at the cutbacks to VIA Rail. We look at the cutbacks in the CBC. It didn't worry about the regions. It just said: "Let us cut" and that is it. We look at lay-offs in Marine Atlantic; we look at the GST. Rural Canada is what gave Canada its uniqueness and it is a necessary item. To any government in office it is necessary. It is necessary that the government take care of rural Canada. It is a must.
We look at what is happening in the fisheries on the east coast. We have heard a lot about the east coast, but look at what is happening on the west coast as well. There are problems with the fisheries on the west coast.
What is wrong in agriculture? There are no family farms any more. People are getting out of farming. Why? We have to preserve those traditions. That is what Canada is all about. That is what will keep us united, our uniqueness. There is nothing wrong with being different. But what is happening is that there is a malaise out there. People in rural Canada feel they have been forgotten.
Maybe the service has not changed in the rural post offices. I am not going to debate that point with the government, because they have their point of view and I have mine. Individuals want to go down to the local post office, meet their friends and have a little chat. They want to go by and see a Canadian flag here and there in their community. For many people in rural Canada there are no Canadian flags flying any more because Canada Post does not exist in their community any more. Canada Post, even if they do exist, are flying a corporate flag now. What is wrong with the Canadian flag?
We are facing an identity crisis. We are facing a crisis in our nation and we are refusing to step up front and say that we are proud to be Canadians. I think to be proud to be a Canadian we would have to go back and look at what has made us Canadians in the true sense. We have to go back and look at our roots. We have to go back and look at rural Canada and say: "We are falling apart here. Let us put it back together. Let us put the programs back in to help rural Canada", not necessarily just throw money at the problem. There is a structural problem and we have to handle it.
I suppose some people would have different ways of doing it, but it is important that we sit down someday and decide how we are going to help rural Canada prosper, how to revitalize it because at the present moment there is a serious problem and we are not handling it very well.
