speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel compelled at this point to note for the benefit of those who may be watching these proceedings on television tonight, that we are actually debating something concrete. What we are debating is a request from the government, in the form of a bill, to borrow $26 billion to keep the machinery of government running over the next fiscal year. That is the amount the government estimates it will need to make up the difference between what it proposes to spend and what it assumes it will receive by way of taxation and other revenues.
The question before us tonight is the third reading of the bill that will authorize the borrowing of that $26 billion. I would like just very briefly to note why I, as the member for Edmonton East, cannot support that request and thus cannot vote for the bill.
March 20, 1991

I would like to start by reminding members that for better than a year and half, in fact, in some instances a lot longer than a year and half, members of the New Democratic Party caucus have been advising the government: "You have to reduce interest rates". The high interest rate policy maintained by the Governor of the Bank of Canada with the delighted acquiescence of the government ministry was crippling the Canadian economy. If those high interest rates were not reduced, unquestionably a recession would be induced and quite possibly it could be a very deep, severe and harmful recession.
That is precisely what has occurred. However, we are now treated with the remarkable spectacle of the finance minister, among others, saying-now that the collapse of the economy has by itself completely destroyed the market for money and thus allowed interest rates to fall, the Minister of Finance and other members of the government are saying- "Well, there you are. We have reduced interest rates".
It is rather like watching the fire truck pull up to the burning house after it has burned to the ground. It is nice to know the fire truck is there, but it is a little late.
If I may extend this little metaphor, what is required now is for the carpenters and the electricians and the roofers and the plasterers to be hired to rebuild the house. We can send the fire truck back to the fire hall. The period of need has passed. What we need now, to make the metaphor plain, is government programs aimed at rebuilding the economy.
That means two things. It means stimulating consumption and it means encouraging new business investment. The budget does neither. The budget discourages consumption by all save the very rich, and has absolutely nothing to encourage business investment in product, plant and equipment.
We are left asking ourselves why the heck then do we need to borrow $26 billion, $1,000 for every man, woman, and child in this country? I regret to say, the answer is what makes it impossible for me to support this bill.
The answer as to why we need to borrow that money is precisely to continue to let the good times roll for Tom d'Aquino's Business Council on National Issues, for
Government Orders
whom the ministry and its supporters opposite constitute so effective a fan club.
For several weeks now, members of my party in this House, most notably the member for Winnipeg-Trans-cona, have been pointing out to the Minister of Finance and other members of the government that, in a budget that is virtually an assault on the wallets, well-being and standard of living of the Canadian people, there is one group that has got off scot free. There is one group that has not been called upon-in the heroic words of the finance minister-to share the burden. It is that small group of Canadians sufficiently wealthy to take advantage of the tax breaks that are there for the rich and the super-rich and the corporations they hold.
In the last couple of weeks, the member for Winnipeg-Transcona has identified five such key loopholes. They are the capital gains lifetime exemption and preferred rates, which will cost the treasury $2.8 billion all by itself. That is enough to exempt the entire population of Alberta from that $1,000 a head required by the borrowing bill.
The business and entertainment tax deduction-the famous three-martini lunch, the box seats for the favoured of the corporate elite that the member for Essex-Windsor was speaking of earlier-that accounts for $1.1 billion a year. The dividend tax credit is another $1 billion a year. The manufacturing and processing tax credit, that gift to the corporate sector which was otherwise so grievously inconvenienced by the manufacturers' sales tax-that is what we were told during the period when the GST was being hawked-that remains, and it is worth another billion dollars a year to those corporations. The interest deductibility rule is all by itself worth $800 million to the wealthy in this country.
Those five considerations alone add up to $6.7 billion. That is better than one-quarter of the entire borrowing requirement identified in the bill. If those loopholes were closed-and closing them would not hurt ordinary Canadians, would not hurt the overwhelming majority of constituents of Edmonton East whom I represent, or the overwhelming majority of constituents of Edmonton North whom you, Mr. Speaker, represent-that borrowing bill could be cut by at least one-quarter. That is real money we are talking about here. There is more.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
In its unfettered pursuit of good times for the rich, the continued program of tax reform that this government has pursued has made more inequitable, more uneven, more unfair what was already an unfair income tax system bequeathed to it by previous Liberal governments.
If I may offer a little aside, I was astonished to hear the hon. member for Restigouche a few moments earlier berate the government for making more inequitable the relative shares paid by the corporate sector through the income tax levied on it as opposed to individual Canadians and the income tax levied on them. It is mostly successive Liberal, but as well Conservative, governments since the 1950s that have taken what was a 50-50 share of income taxes paid-and it is virtually a straight line progression-to what is now 90 per cent collected from individuals and 10 per cent collected from corporations.
It is grossly inequitable. For a member of the Liberal caucus to get up and complain about it strikes me as hubris of a truly Homeric scope.
Just to make this point clear, I note that the most recent book of stats we have on personal income tax was published last fall covering the taxation year 1988, which you will recall, Mr. Speaker, is the first year of the much heralded income tax reform. It was when the finance minister's changes to the income tax system were supposed to take effect and make things a whole lot fairer for all Canadians. This book now lets us see what actually happened.
Do you know what happened? What happened-to the surprise of some, I suppose; to the surprise of none in my caucus-was that the income tax system became more unfair. In fact, the average tax paid by Canadians making more than a quarter of a million dollars a year-of those who paid tax-from 1987 to 1988 dropped by 15 per cent. It dropped $20,597. The average tax paid by those earning a quarter of a million dollars a year or more went down.
What happened on the other end? The average tax paid by those making 15 grand a year or less, from 1987 to the first year of tax reform in 1988, went up by 13 per cent, or $71. By any dispassionate measure, that is grossly unfair.
Just to rub salt in the wound, the same year the number of those Canadians earning a quarter of a
million dollars or more who paid no tax went up by 40 per cent from the previous year. In 1988 we had 140 Canadians who made a quarter of a million dollars a year or more and did not pay a penny on it, not one red cent. Those earning 50 grand a year or more who paid no tax went up 87 per cent, to 5,430. That is one whale of a tax reform. That is one heck of an example of fairness.
I would suggest that no Canadian who has been paying attention is going to be surprised by these numbers. It is just a continuation of the policy of ever greater unfairness in the taxation system that has been pursued by successive Liberal and Conservative governments since the end of the Second World War.
It is my constituents in Edmonton East, the folk who work at the chemical plants, the folk who work at Gainers, the folk who work in the public sector in the schools and in the federal government offices, who are being made to pay more and more so that the rich can pay less and less.
That is why I, on their behalf, cannot support this borrowing bill.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with this bill, the government is asking the House the authority to borrow $26 billion, $400 million of which for the 1991-1992 financial year. This request, made necessary by this government's policies over the past few years, must be set in the context of the projections contained in the last budget.
Obviously, the government failed to reduce the deficit after promising to do it. Now, it is presenting a budget that goes against the role traditionally played by the federal government during a recession.
Of course, we are aware of the phenomenal size of the accumulated national debt and the deficit which is remaining high in spite of the repeated promises of the Minister of Finance. We knew that there was little leeway and that not much could be expected from the last budget. Still, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance managed to disappoint us on three grounds. First, the Minister of Finance took no responsibility for the present situation. Second, the measures announced in this budget will deepen the recession and prevent the economy from making a strong recovery. Third, chances of finding effective long-term solutions are very slim.
March 20, 1991

What responsibility does this government have in the current national finance crisis? For seven years now, the Minister of Finance has been posing as the brave white knight trying to improve a disastrous situation inherited from the Liberals. I have no qualms about condemning the Liberal mismanagement but, as the years go by, the minister must come to realize that his government also made major mistakes that contributed to a large extent to the deterioration of our national finances.
Let me give a few examples of mistakes that were later corrected. There was the $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption introduced by the Conservatives, not the Liberals. This exemption even applied to capital gains made on rental properties, which brought speculative pressure to bear on those properties without attracting productives investment. The government has to backtrack and reduce the exemption to $100,000.
Another example is VIA Rail. While the Liberal government had the courage to propose the required streamlining plan, this government, when it came to power, was only too eager to cancel it and reallocate hundreds of thousands of dollars to a recovery plan that failed. But they finally carried out the streamlining planned by the Liberals. What was ironic was to see the former minister, the hon. Jean-Luc Pepin, become the major advocate of this government which was carrying out his plan five years too late.
There are many other examples, but I am more concerned, Mr. Speaker, about the mistakes that were not recognized. Think of the Hibernia project for instance. More than $2 billion in federal government funds were pumped into a venture that will never be profitable and which will require more enormous capital outlays to be kept afloat in the years to come. In addition to not being viable, the project's potential for damage to the environment is far greater than in the case of hydroelectric projects.
Actually, the Lower Churchill project, which is marking time as a result of the Newfoundland government's stubborn position, would have created more jobs than the Hibernia project, without government subsidies and with minimal risk to the environment.
Government Orders
How are we supposed to make sense of a decision, that includes the construction of a new shipyard in Newfoundland, at a time when Canadian shipyards are losing money and the industry has been subject to costly restructuring during the past ten years? The present problems at Versatile in Vancouver are just one more episode in the restructuring process we already experienced in Quebec. In fact, Davie Shipbuilding in Levis, which is technically bankrupt, is still waiting for the federal government's decision, which keeps being postponed, to give the green light so it can continue work on its defence contracts.
The shipyards under construction in Newfoundland will never be viable. How can the Minister of Finance defend such wasteful policies? Is this a sensible way to manage the country's finances? I may add that the Liberals' support for getting the necessary legislation through the House of Commons and the Senate is certainly no guarantee for good management. This is electioneering at public expense.
After seven years, the Minister of Finance can no longer deny his responsibility for the deplorable state of the nation's finances. He must take the responsibility for his government's decisions.
And now, what about the future first of all, the immediate future. What is the government doing to get us out of the recession? Nothing. In fact, it is increasing pressure on wage earners. The most intolerable measure in this entire budget is probably the 24.5 per cent increase in unemployment insurance premiums. This is a clear incentive to increase lay-offs and unemployment. This comes at a time when the minister says one of the major problems in our economy is that our labour costs are higher than those of our competitors. So why increase them in the middle of a recession? I found only one explanation, in the speech made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration when she introduced this bill. She said that if premiums had not been increased this year, and I quote: "The expected deficit in the UI account would have required large premium increases in 1993". Economically speaking, this alternative would have been entirely acceptable, since in 1993, we should be in the middle of an economic recovery. So why not wait until then? Probably for political reasons.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
In spite of the polls and the desertions, the government hopes to stretch its mandate up to 1993. Election logic has clearly won over economic logic.
Another cut, that of $70 million in the subsidies to non-profit organizations dedicated to help the needy, is also unacceptable in the present context. In fact, we were not expecting miracles from the Minister of Finance. We are aware of the difficulties involved in public finances. On the other hand, when election logic prevails over a minimum of compassion for the unemployed and the poor in the present situation, it must be denounced Mr. Speaker. But let us look further.
Are there in this budget directions which would indicate that the government will seriously deal with the basic reasons behind the chronic deficit as well as the very ineffectiveness of the federal system. Unfortunately, the answer is no. The government is making cuts everywhere, but maintains its determination to meddle in all aspects of the lives of the people and the provinces. We are back to the era of liberal centralization which built a political and bureaucratic structure which is forever creating deficits, unless the provinces and the people demand a quick change in policy.
Remember the Tory government which preached both decentralization and consultation! Where are we now? By systematically cutting in transfer payments to the provinces, the Tory government decentralized the accounts payable, while maintaining and even increasing its control over the taxation areas. Now that it is no longer able to pay, does the federal government intend to return to the provinces their areas of jurisdiction? No at all; quite the contrary. It intends to introduce new legislation, especially in the health care area, to increase its powers. It intends to give itself the powers it needs to compel others to spend while imposing its own national standards.
Is that the only area, Mr. Speaker? Not at all. Read again the speech which the Minister of Employment and Immigration made when she introduced her bill on March 5 last. She explained her manpower enhancement strategy by saying and I quote: "Our strategy is based on the idea of partnerships; partnerships with employers, with labour, with education and with provinces and territories."
After reminding the House of the announcement concerning the new Canadain Labour Force Development Board, she exclaimed, and I quote: "What a breakthrough for Canada, to be able to build the kind of partnership that is going to be needed in the decade ahead". What breakthrough is the minister talking about?
She talks about a fresh initiative, a new intrusion on the part of the federal government which, no longer financially strong enough to maintain its presence in the vocational training field, chose to grab the unemployment insurance funds and re-affirm its intention to continue with the kind of jurisdiction duplications that led to the wanton resource wastes of which we are all aware. In Quebec, all groups representing management, labour and teachers have refused to sit on this board. They are all in favour of the Government of Quebec repatriating all powers in the field of vocational training. What success is the minister referring to? It is in fact a failure, a new confrontation, yet another example of federal arrogance.
Whatever happened to the willingness of the Conservative government to decentralize? After a few years we have to admit that the willingness has disappeared and been replaced by the old Liberal arrogance. The speeches of the Prime Minister increasingly attest to that fact. Should we be surprised? Who have been his closest advisers in recent months? The likes of Tellier, Dicemey, Gagne and Tasse, the best soldiers Trudeau had to send to the front lines in the referendum battle, a team that is quite prepared to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to maintain an outdated vision of the way to govern this country, a team whose sole aim is to hang on to the power of the federal government's bureaucratic and political machine, not to give this country the political and economic institutions that would meet the aspirations of the Canadian public.
The economic failure of the federal government cannot hide the political failure. The political reality of this country is that it is made up of two nations, two peoples that must quickly undertake an in-depth review of their political and economic institutions. Of course, when the Conservative government came into office, we were hoping for progress in that direction.
March 20, 1991

But with the Meech Lake failure, confrontation is the order of the day. Quite clearly, the Prime Minister and his government are doing exactly what the Liberal Party did in the past. I am utterly convinced, Mr. Speaker, that that is not what Canadians and Quebeckers are wishing for. Bureaucracy and the federal government's policy have become the main obstacles preventing Quebeckers and Canadians from reaching an agreement. And we will be working relentlessly in the next few months to reach such agreements.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened well to the Hon. Member for Rosemont. He referred earlier to VIA Rail. When talking either about engines or workers,-I come from a distant area-when talking about the railway line between Senneterre and Montreal and back Montreal-Senneterre-Cochrane and Shawi-nigan, the way my good friend the Hon. Member for Shawinigan, Denis Pronovost, pronounces it, something must be said. We are reaping what the Liberals have sown. After investigation, the House will remember that the line from Senneterre-Cochrane provides $60,000 in revenues, while it costs a million dollar a year to adminster VIA Rail from Senneterre-Cochrane. Yet, there is something strange. As Members of the Opposition, whether within the Liberal Party or the NDP-and even you who are part of the Bloc Quebecois, although you were elected under the Conservative banner-you accepted a number of things when you were elected. Mr. Speaker, one thing must be said: The VIA Rail passenger train often arrives in Senneterre. But the administrators of this Crown Corporation do not have even the teams they need to drive the train to Amos, La Sarre and Cochrane- Often, however, VIA management doesn't even have a crew to run the locomotive, to go to Amos, La Sarre and Cochrane. I never saw anything like it. That's VIA management for you. It's not the government's fault. This is a Crown corporation.
You mentioned Meech and the fact that we lost everything. I, for one, hope that Quebeckers are pleased with the Canada-Quebec agreement referred to in Meech, the agreement that has just been signed by the federal government and the Government of Quebec, the Canada-Quebec agreement on immigration. The people in our area are pleased with this agreement.
Government Orders
You also referred to the Minister of Finance and his Budget, when you said we had lost everything. Thanks to the Conservative members from Quebec, thanks to the Quebec caucus, Quebec was able to patriate a number of things that were here in Ottawa, including a research laboratory we got in Abitibi. This had never been done before. The Liberals never did it. The NDP never supported us in this respect, and the Bloc Quebecois certainly never gave us their support when it came to patriating research and development.
There is another item I would like to mention in my comments, and that is the matter of isolated post allowances. This was a very positive development for workers, for union members, for all the workers in Matagami, Joutel, Lebel-sur-Quevillon, Chapais Chi-bougamau. Now they have isolation benefits. That is an important development.
I noticed recently Mr. Speaker, that members of the Bloc Quebecois keep saying they are defending the rights of Quebeckers. I just made a speech on March 7 on the subject of the precautionary withdrawal from work for pregnant women in federally regulated businesses. Well, there are a lot of women in Quebec who work for unions like the FTQ, the CSN, the Metal Workers, but in this debate on the defence of pregnant women, in the federally regulated businesses, the Bloc Quebecois was nowhere to be seen. They never defended us.

Why not have waited until 1993 to increase the unemployment insurance premiums? Because the Conservatives hope that 1993 will be an election year. That is why. This is where electoral considerations took precedence over economic considerations. That is the problem.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am delighted to have the opportunity to speak during consideration of this stage of Bill C-97, an act to provide borrowing authority. Billions of dollars are to be borrowed to feed an insatiable appetite of a government that knows not what it is doing.
My colleagues on this side of the House have done an admirable job of pointing out the inadequacies of this budget and of laying bare the very twisted ideology which drives this government to deliver blows time and again to the people of this country. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to add my voice to this debate at this time.
As for the defence of workers, you know, the hon. member for Abitibi is a very sympathetic and hard-working member, whom I respect, but if he really takes to heart the workers' interests, I wonder how the Conservative members from Quebec could vote against the antiscab legislation put forward by the Bloc Quebecois-

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: I voted for it.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Yes, I know you voted for it yourself, but your colleagues voted against it. That is why it was defeated.
I agree with you totally that mortgage rates are much better than they were in 1982. It was an absolute disaster in 1982! I agree that, because of the very tight management by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, we now have relatively stable long-term rates. Putting the brakes suddenly is what threw us in a much deeper recession- the Governor of the Bank himself admitted it. I am not blaming it all on him. It was indeed hard to predict, but the Governor did decide to apply the brakes even though everyone was anticipating a recession. Today, he admits that he should have changed course earlier, but we are already in a deep recession.
I would be the first person in this House to say that we need fiscal accountability and responsibility in government; there is no doubt about it. I would be the first to say that we must all do our share to rid our country of the deficit so that future generations are not saddled with paying for the government's impetuous spending habits.
However, let us begin by looking at the situation in the manufacturing sector and how the policies of this government in its repeated budgetary fiascos has snuffed out the fires in the so-called "engine of Canada's economy-the province of Ontario".
It would come as no surprise to many Canadians outside Ontario that it is actually this province that is feeling the greatest pinch during these difficult economic times. According to the findings of a Liberal task force, Ontario accounts for four out of every ten lost Canadian jobs. Ontario is now feeling the greatest impact with respect to plant closures, bankruptcies, unemployment and the general economic slowdown.
The issues which are consistently cited as reasons for the dramatic downturn in the economy are: high interest rates, Canada's artificially high dollar, high rate of taxation compounded by the GST, the negative effects of the free trade agreement, and the government's mismanagement of the federal debt.

March 20, 1991

Here in the national capital region, which my riding of Nepean and my constituents are a part of, we were once known for economic stability. We in the nation's capital are not immune any more to the effects of this government's economic policies, as a shrinking and demoralized Public Service, bankruptcies and rising unemployment in the region all add up to a greater reliance on already strained social service agencies.
In essence, we in the nation's capital are suffering from the trickle down effect, at a time of increasing dependence on social assistance programs brought on by this government's policies. We are watching those programs dry up due to a lack of funding by this government.
In straight economic terms, this budget and this government are costing Canadians dearly, but it is the human cost that is most tragic. The real tragedy is that this government conveniently glosses over the hardships which it has inflicted on Canadians. Middle-class Canadians are taxed to death. They are generally unable to enjoy the same tax loopholes which rich friends of this government enjoy.
Women continue to struggle toward true equality in our society. The government causes further setbacks by cutting funding and programs which might assist women in their cause. In some ways the plight of women has grown worse, not better, under this administration.
It is a well documented fact that the incidence of family violence and family breakdown increases as financial pressures mount. We can be sure that every Canadian family is feeling the bite of the hard economic times brought on by the policies of the government. It is almost always women who are at the receiving end of family violence.
Even then I suspect that a solution would involve a glitzy public relations campaign designed to gloss over the problems of increasing family breakdown and violence against women.
Next in the line of this government's fire are the children. There are approximately 100 million children today living in poverty in Canada and close to 200,000 of them must rely on food banks for their daily bread. That is unconscionable.
Government Orders
I ask: What kind of future will these children have if all they ever know is poverty, hunger and hopelessness? Undernourished, they find it difficult to learn. Many of them will end up by dropping out of school or certainly not doing as well as they could if given better circumstances in which to grow and learn. They will become part of a vicious perpetual cycle of poverty. They will know nothing else. They will grow up with a deeply rooted sense of cynicism and mistrust.
The government which claims to despise the so-called welfare state mentality is actually creating a much greater malaise. Once entrenched, there will be no social safety net to prevent the fall of all of the people who will be in its grip.
This all comes at a time when an international agreement to which 30-some countries throughout the world agreed was signed last May: the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. We may recall that the Prime Minister of Canada went to Washington and chaired, I believe, that committee. We were all so enthused and pleased that Canada was going to be involved.
To this date, Canada has not signed the agreement. What a farce: travelling to Washington, all this hoop-la, chair the committee, and then he does not sign the agreement. It outlines minimum standards for children, among other things, in health care and education. It encourages the development of different forms of secondary education systems both general and vocational. It ensures appropriate health care, family planning and education. This should be available and accessible to all children. The list goes on and on. I could cite many examples.
Does this government expect that the provinces are going to submit happily to spending even more money in the areas of health care and education at a time when the federal government is cutting them off?
I was delighted when Canada agreed to be part of this convention. I do not know what has gone wrong. I would encourage all members on the opposite side of the House to put pressure on their cabinet, on the people who have the power to issue a signature in Washington on the rights of the child.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
The public servants of this country have also been singled out for punishment in the budget. Not since this government attempted to deindex old age pensions have I seen a more direct and cynical attack on a specific sector of society. This government believes that Canadians feel their public servants are nothing more than overpaid and underproductive bureaucrats.
The government, by its actions, is telling every employer in Canada that it is acceptable to throw away the right to bargain and it is acceptable to hold over the heads of the workers the threats of job losses and contracting out. Women in the Public Service have also been hurt.
Another sector which is carrying more than its share of this country's economic burden is small business. Any small business that has managed to survive the recession, which this government has created and now ignores, deserve a medal of valour for they have survived a war that has been waged against them by their own government. They are now required, along with the employee, to pay all the unemployment insurance bills. The federal government is no longer paying part of that program. Eighty per cent of new jobs in this country are created by small business and yet this government will turn around and stick a knife in its back.
I had a call from a plumber recently with regards to the FST. He said: "I thought when GST was implemented that I would no longer have to pay the FST." His supplier was charging him for both. He said: "I cannot afford it. What do I do?" I phoned Revenue Canada, and what did it tell me: "The marketplace will sort all this out." In the meantime, there is a plumber who cannot pay for his supplies because someone had refused to remove the FST. It is a paperwork jungle for the small business person. The GST has created horrendous problems.
The finance minister and the Prime Minister are being less than truthful when they say this is a budget aimed at deficit elimination.
Actually they are passing the buck to the provinces, the municipalities and, through the back door route, to the taxpayers of this country. We are already overtaxed; programs to help women, the unemployed, the disadvantaged, have been slashed. Now this government in this budget has furthered its vicious assault on our health
care and education programs. It has pitted workers against each other, and it has left the provinces and municipalities holding the bag.
Yesterday, the Canadian Human Rights Commission released its 1990 annual report. It has made recommendations in several areas which require action, not cuts; aboriginal issues; in issues affecting the disabled; with respect to women, immigrants, visible minorities. Many of the recommendations in the report have been on the books for five years or longer. In other words, every year, the Human Rights Commission is recommending these things and the government is doing nothing about it.
The report calls for the acknowledgement of the government of debts owed to aboriginal people. Some 41 per cent of unattached women 65 years of age and older continue to remain below the poverty line, despite a recommendation contained in the 20 year old report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada. When will these women get their due?
The commission report calls for measures to foster improved race relations, yet the pieces of pie for all groups and programs working toward this end, get smaller and smaller.
This government has further proven that it, and its policies, are incapable of saving, let alone building, this nation. This government should try to use some creativity and imagination in attempting to solve our nation's problems. Let us provide, not cut, training and education to get people back to work.
One of the things I have been doing recently in my riding, and I started about six weeks ago, is meeting with the business community. Appointments are set and I meet people from the business community on an average of three businesses a week for an hour, sometimes up to two hours in the morning. I have met with companies as large as Northern Telecom, which employs 3,000 people in the city of Nepean and I have also met smaller businesses that employ maybe only 10 people.
Without fail, the business community is saying to me that this government is destroying business in this country. They cannot compete because of the policies of this government. Some 90 per cent of their business is now outside of the country because they cannot compete within their own country.
March 20, 1991

A company I visited yesterday has computer systems in the House of Representatives and the Congress in Washington. Do you think he can get something into the Parliament of Canada or in the House of Commons? Not on your life. He told me of the paperwork, the bureaucratic red tape. This gentleman said to me: "I could ciy when I see what this government is doing to business in Canada".
Let us provide adequate health care so that people can feel secure and get on with living. Let us reform our system of taxation to a more fair and level playing field, so that the average Canadian does not feel cynical and over-burdened. Let us create a fair justice system so that people do not feel persecuted and resentful.
I say to the government, I say to the Prime Minister, and I say to the Minister of Finance: let us invest in people, and they will give us back much more. We will have a better country. They can spend their time and energy just getting on with living, rather than spending their time and energy resenting the government and each other for their difficult predicament.
This approach, in addition to solving the economic woes of this country, would go a long way toward promoting national unity. The two major issues that I see in the country today are national unity and the economic problems we are faced with. In many ways they probably go hand in hand. With a positive outlook, and with a hand-in-glove approach to the people of Canada, I think we can succeed. We are a great nation. We have a wonderful future, and I think we have to be sympathetic. We have to get to the grass roots and find out what people are hearing, find out what they are saying, find out what they are feeling, and continue to build this great nation.

But then she proceeded for the next 15 minutes to discuss item after item after item in which the government would have to pay out more money, not less, that would be adding more to the burden, not only to the

taxpayers we have now, but more burden to the taxpayers we are going to have in the future, the young people, the people who are truly our future in Canada.
I would like to ask the hon. member to contemplate that situation. Could she go back to her opening statement and indicate to the House and to the people who are watching, how she would propose to achieve all of the things she mentioned, and yet still be responsible to the country, to the taxpayers today and the young people who are going to inherit the debt that we do not pay.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the gentleman for his question.
I would like to go back to the years 1984 to 1988. Canada had, in those four years, the largest unprecedented growth in its history. In other words, the growth over the anticipated revenue was so large and so massive that it never before happened in the history of this country. That was during the first term this government held office in Canada. Did it reduce one dollar of the deficit? Not on your life. And do you think I can find out what it did with all that money during that time? No, sir, I cannot, because the books are closed to me as an opposition member. This government had billions and billions of dollars, I believe it was something like $100 billion, in excess revenue over anticipated revenue in those four years and it doubled the debt in that time.
What do I say to the member sitting opposite me? If he cannot manage the economy in the good times, and here we are in the tight times and he wants to impose a GST when everybody is already in a tight situation. He wants to increase taxes. In other words, hit a guy when he is down. Oh, sure, hit a guy when he is down and see what it is like. Why did you not hit them when they were up, when we were up those four years. You are poor managers. You do not know how to manage the economy.
For instance, money should be poured into research and the education system. Every one of those businesses I have been attending mentioned this. Northern Telecom used to hire the top ten percentile from the University of Waterloo. They are not staying in this country any more, they are going to the States. Do you know why? Because we are over-taxed in this country. They will not stay here. They can earn $50,000 in the United States and it is worth $100,000 here in Canada. We cannot compete. We are losing our students to the American sector.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
Another thing that was mentioned was to hire an American engineer and bring him to Canada. In order for that same engineer who might be making $40,000 in the States, to bring him to Canada to work for a company like Northern Telecom, they have to pay him $75,000. They cannot afford it any more.
Mr. Speaker, while I appreciate the gentleman's question to me, I find it absolutely incredulous that here are people who are unemployed, their incomes have been cut and we are wanting to hit them even harder with the high interest rates, with the GST, with all of the other cutbacks in the programs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak on the estimates and the budget. The finance minister's budget is a continuation of this government's destructive economic policies. As is the case in all regions of Canada, those living in the Hamilton area are suffering from the made-in-Canada recession.
On January 23 and 24, as chairman of the Hamilton-Niagara caucus, I conducted hearings on the economy and the recession. The participation of the hon. members from Hamilton East, Hamilton West, Haldimand- Norfolk, Etobicoke North, Welland-St. Catharines-Thorold, and London East in the task force on the economy and the recession contributed a great deal toward its success.
We heard from 25 groups and individuals representing a cross section of the community: social service groups, labour unions, food banks, hospitals, small businesses, Mohawk College and McMaster University, low cost housing organizations, the construction industry, and the steel industry, among others. The presentations that we heard put a human face on the cold statistics that we hear in this House day after day.
The citizens of the Hamilton area painted a grim picture of how the region is suffering as a result of this government's policies. It was amazing that witness after witness, representing interests from across the spectrum, all expressed deep concern about the direction this government is leading us. In this time of great national division, the one unifying factor may be the Canadian public's rejection of this government's economic policies.
The shocking thing is that there is nothing accidental about what the government has done, nor is the current recession the result of global factors. This is the Prime Minister's one truly Canadian effort: a made-in-Canada recession. The Prime Minister even bragged last fall about engineering an economic slowdown. Despite his many other failed initiatives, I must admit that on this one the Prime Minister has really outdone himself.
This recession is the result of very deliberate actions by this government. The government's high interest rate policy, for example, is hitting all sectors of the Hamilton economy. Traditionally, Canadian interest rates have been 1 to 2 per cent over their American counterparts. Over the last year, Canadian interest rates have been 4 to 5 per cent higher than those of the United States. This has prevented young families from buying homes, has forced companies to lay off workers, and has prevented small businesses from expanding.
If the government is not prepared to go out and hear what Canadians have to say about their economic policies, then let me make it easier for them by repeating what my colleagues and I were told by witnesses at the task force in Hamilton.
Family Services of Hamilton-Wentworth described at the hearings what high interest rates are doing to young families:
This stage of the family life cycle is marked by high rates of borrowing and low rates of saving, due to the demands of household formation. As a result, young families are affected by the higher costs of borrowing but receive few of the benefits of the high rates of return on saving.
Alderman Don Ross, chairman of the Hamilton-Wentworth Economic Development Committee, offered the following overview of the problem.
For improved economy we need the Bank of Canada to reduce interest rates to a level that will enable people, industry, and commerce to feel comfortable enough to re-invest in major capital projects; whether that be a new car, plant or merchandise.
March 20, 1991

Bob Crockford, chairman of the Hamilton branch of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, raised further concerns with respect to the manufacturers' spending on capital investment.
- the loss of manufacturing investment may be the single greatest
cost of the government's high interest rate policy.
Cameron Nolan of the Hamilton Construction Association described the effects of high interest rates on the construction industry.
The result has been slower growth and resulting unemployment - Our industry urges the federal government -to amend its interest rate policy to one which calls for reducing interest rates. A reduction will bring us out of the recession.
The Hamilton and District Chamber of Commerce in their presentation focused on the high Canadian dollar:
The high cost of the Canadian dollar is impeding the country's ability to sustain its export capabilities in world markets.
The introduction of the goods and services tax in the middle of a recession has only served to make a bad situation worse for those in the Hamilton area. By pulling dollars out of an already depressed economy, the GST has dealt a severe blow to the Hamilton area.
Scott Jacks, owner of a small Hamilton natural food store described what the goods and services tax will do to small business:
Many small businesses find cash flow to be a difficult challenge at the best of times. I must point out that the GST could have a devastating effect on cash flow, even to the point of putting someone out of business.
The wonderful prosperity the Prime Minister predicted under free trade has unfortunately not been apparent anywhere north of the 49th parallel. Since the signing of the free trade agreement there has been a flight of Canadian jobs to the United States. Stelco in its presentation at our hearings noted the increased difficulties in doing business as more and more of its customers are closing their doors and moving production to the United States.
Ed Herchuk, president of the Ontario Council of Labour, told us that under the free trade agreement American construction workers are enjoying far greater rights in cross border work than Canadian labourers and as a result "they daily take jobs away from Canadian construction workers".
Government Orders
The deliberate policies of the federal government have all contributed to the deindustrialization of Ontario, the heartland of Canadian industry. The effects are as clear as they are shocking.
In the last year unemployment has doubled in the Hamilton area. Today there are 30,000 Hamiltonians out of work. For the Prime Minister's benefit, that is more people than live in his home town of Baie Comeau.
Consumer bankruptcies in Hamilton shot up to 1,062 in 1990, an 80 per cent increase over 1989. Business bankruptcies went up 30 per cent during the same period.
Food banks in Hamilton now report approximately 20,000 people using their services each month. Social service agencies report a 67 per cent increase in the case load in the Hamilton-Wentworth region. Line-ups for social assistance housing continue to rise.
And how, Mr. Speaker, in this budget has this government addressed the concerns so eloquently expressed by the witnesses at the Hamilton task force hearings? Obviously, it is not concerned. For example, under this year's budget job retraining funds were cut by $100 million. It is small wonder unemployment has risen 10.2 per cent, just as the Minister of Finance predicted. Hamiltonians only wish he could have been as accurate with his predictions of economic prosperity in the last election.
Another example of the government's lack of concern is with consumers and businesses already struggling due to the GST and high interest rates, the finance minister has decided to hike unemployment insurance premiums by 24 per cent. Funds for social assistance housing have been slashed.
This budget will not only worsen the current economic recession in Hamilton, but it will also prevent Hamiltonians and all Canadians from improving their situation in the long run. Cuts in transfer payments to post-secondary education will hurt our universities and colleges and make it even more difficult for us to compete in the global market.
This government has declared war on Canadians with high inflation, high interest rates and general misman-

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have a chance to speak in opposition to Bill C-97 by which the government intends to borrow $26.4 billion from the Canadian people and of course, saddle them with still more taxes to pay the interest to those rich Canadians who lend the government the money.
This $26.4 billion is something in the range of $1,500 per year for every Canadian family. The government does it very lightly. This government is not listening to the Canadian people. We can see that by the way the Canadian people rate the government at the bottom of the polls.
It has been cutting taxes on the rich. It has been raising taxes on the poor. It has been cutting the unemployment insurance benefits at a time when it knows that unemployment is going to rise. It has been giving Canadian jobs away to the United States and other countries through the free trade agreement, giving jobs away to corporations that take them to the United States as they took 600 jobs away from the Inglis washing machine plant in Trinity-Spadina within a year of the free trade agreement by lowering the tariffs, or to U.S. based companies for the most part that contract those jobs out to very low wage countries of the Third World.
It has not been listening to the Canadian people about its war spending during 1990 and 1991. It has not been listening to the Canadian people about the many, many millions of dollars that it spent oppressing the native people with the Canadian army around the Oka dispute.
We have all read in our public and high school history about how the English people three and a half centuries ago decided it was time to tell the king and the other rich landed gentry that they did not have the right to raise taxes on the king's whim and to spend the money on the king's whim. They argued that the king did not have the right. He said he did, he had the divine right, that he was made king by the decision of God. Therefore whatever he did had the authority of God. The people did not believe him and under Cromwell they were willing to fight to tell the king that he not only did not have the right, but that he did not have the power. To prove their point, they cut off his head.
Then for a while England became governed more by democratic means through the parliamentary system. But in the last couple of decades this Parliament has been losing even the limited power that it has had. That is to say, the people who are elected to this Parliament as members, constituency by constituency, have less and less control over what this government does. This government makes wildly false promises during election time that it clearly does not intend to keep.
While I was in Mexico last week, I found it interesting to hear the President of Mexico, through the media, solemnly promising that he would not give up one iota of Mexico's control over its natural oil and resources, solemnly promising that he would not make any trade deals that would bring contracts or jobs into Mexico that would damage the environment and so on. It all sounds dismally familiar on the basis of what we heard three years ago from this government. We heard, in 1984 when this government was seeking election, it promise solemnly that it would have nothing to do with a trade deal with the United States because it would be a marriage of the elephant and the mouse and when the elephant roles over, the now Prime Minister said it would be the finish of the mouse.
They deceived the voters at election time and then when representatives elected here to Parliament complained about what the government was doing and used this forum to explain to the people how the government has deceived people, the government used a gag. It has gagged this Parliament more times in the last six years than all governments did before it. It even has the nerve to spend millions and millions of tax dollars, further deceiving the people, as it tried to deceive the people about Bill C-55, the anti-refugee law it introduced three and a half years ago, with misleading, quite false interpretations of it, as it did last year, putting out millions of dollars to mislead people about the goods and services tax which was thoroughly unpopular.
My point is that Canadians have been losing control of their government. We still have the right to vote at election time. They did in Samosa's Nicaragua. They do in the ARENA parties in El Salvador. They can come and vote, but those people under Samosa in Nicaragua and under the ARENA party now in El Salvador do not control their government through that vote.
March 20,1991

In Canada it a little more subtle. By law, for example, Canadian people are prevented from acting, through the members of Parliament, to decide whether Canada goes to war. Last year this government sent ships, planes and troops to the Middle East without consulting the Canadian people through their elected representatives. For six weeks Canadians and members of Parliament asked the government to convene Parliament.
There was a little concern about 174 unarmed people with dark skins landing in Nova Scotia. The government declared it an emergency. It talked about an invasion. You would think we were being invaded by thousands of troops armed with machine guns and tanks-174 dark skinned people wading ashore in Nova Scotia was an emergency. Parliament was recalled. A law was passed authorizing the Canadian government to commit piracy on the high seas by seizing ships and turning them away in waters that Canada does not own.
But when the government is going to spend millions upon million upon millions of dollars on a war project in the Middle East, it is no emergency. The government did not use the emergences act which it passed. It sneaked around the comers instead and in connivance, not with the premiers, but with the business interests who profit by war, it simply sent the ships and then later recalled Parliament, not really to give permission, but only to give loyal support, which the government majority gave.
In the same way, it never asked Parliament for permission to send the troops against Oka, a dispute which could have been settled any time in the last 200 years by fair negotiation with the people who lived here before we Europeans came.
Later, after it was all finished, it asked Parliament and its tame majority to pass a resolution approving it. But there was a long, long struggle for months before there was any willingness to have a parliamentary committee open up the facts.
Again in 1991, when President Bush pressured the United Nations Security Council-not the United Nations General Assembly, the only really democratic body of the United Nations, but the Security Council, controlled by a few holdovers from the power system 45 years ago -to pass an ambiguous resolution which President Bush interpreted as authorization for war, it scrapped the sanctions, which were working, because President Bush wanted war. This government delayed recalling Parliament. The American Congress came back
Government Orders
to debate it before the bombing began. This Parliament was not allowed to begin debate until the bombing was already upon us.
It made a mockery of this Parliament in that debate. It made a mockery of the speaking and made a mockery of voting.
In Cromwell's time, England was ruled by the rich nobility and the king. It was the merchants, the working classes in London and many of the peasants in the countryside who provided the strength of Cromwell's army which ended that rule.
Canada is now ruled by the Business Council on National Issues, the chief executives of 150 of the largest corporations in Canada. They called for three things: they called for a trade deal, they got it; they called for cuts in the social programs and they are getting it; they called for a boost in the arms budget and they are getting it. Those are the ones who call the tune in this country, not the Canadian people.
It is wider than this. It is not just a matter of Canada alone. Canada has its allies, that is to say this government has its allies. When the Prime Minister was elected the first time, practically the first act he did was to go to the White House to take his orders from President Reagan. Now he does the same with President Bush and the American arms manufacturers and their junior partners in Canada.
Another of the allies of Canada is the landed oligarchy and the army that control El Salvador, not that Canada gives direct aid there except for a few million dollars that it gives indirectly through a so-called aid project, but because Canada keeps silent. Canada keeps silent about the crimes committed by the government of El Salvador and by the army of El Salvador which is armed to the tune of more than a million dollars a day by the government of the United States.
Canada refuses to criticize the U.S. as Canada refused, with one minor exception, to criticize the U.S. proxy war against Nicaragua. Canada refuses to criticize the allies of the United States which maintain corrupt and oppressive regimes, such as the corrupt and wealthy rulers of some of the states in Arabia: the feudal lords and so-called kings in the Middle East who control those oil resources on behalf of the United States and literally for many years past got away with murder.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
Now this government is asking Parliament to agree to lend it $26.4 billion. There will be no control over how it is spent because there is no control either over how it is raised. As my colleagues have pointed out before, one-quarter of that amount, one-quarter of that $26.4 billion could have been saved if the government had closed five of the major loopholes. The capital gains lifetime exemption fuels a great deal of the speculation that raises housing prices in Toronto beyond the reach of ability to pay, but the government gives a tax break of $2.8 billion, nearly $3 billion.
The business entertainment tax deduction, over $1 billion to the people who need it least. They claim they have to compete with others. Jones has to have this subsidy to entertain customers, to take them away from Smith, who has to have the same subsidy to entertain customers to take them away from Jones. They all benefit, all these top business people. But the Canadian working people have to pay extra taxes to feed them in luxury.
The dividend tax credit cushions the taxation that might be levied against the people who live partly off the dividends of corporations.
The manufacturing the processing tax credit amounts to another billion dollars. This was supposed to be done away with by the goods and services tax, but the government played a little bit of a shill game there and just slipped it through anyway.
The interest deductibility rule is another welfare scheme for land speculators. Nearly a billion dollars. The total of this is $6.7 billion, one-quarter of what the government wants to borrow.
Another way of putting it is that two or three years ago, in 1988, the average tax paid by Canadians making more than $225,000 a year went down by over $20,000. Twenty thousand dollars is a lot more than some people make by working for a year in Canada. But these people had $20,000 taken off their taxes, about 15 per cent of their income. At the same time, taxes paid by Canadians earning $15,000 or less rose by $71 which is a hike of 13 per cent.
This is the policy of this government. It could have saved one-quarter of this loan by a fair tax system, but it refused to do it, although this question was raised time and time again in Parliament by our party.
It can save another one-quarter of this loan money, if not right away at least soon, by taking our troops out of Europe. Whatever may have been the argument for putting the troops into Europe 30 and 40 years ago, it is agreed now that there is no threat of the Russian tanks rolling into Berlin and Paris. In fact, they are going the other way. But the government insists on spending over $6 billion to keep those troops there, the direct and indirect costs. It could take that money out. Those people could be more appropriately applied back home in Canada or, if necessary, in peacekeeping operations elsewhere.
As I say, if it could not be done all in one year, it could be begun this year.
Instead, this government has shown that it will get this money by cutting the programs for native people, which are a miserable small part of the obligation that we owe them for the land we took from them; by cutting programs that would benefit women who are still earning no more than two-thirds of what men earn in this country; cutting programs for higher education, pressuring institutions such as the University of Toronto to refuse to bargain in good faith with the men and women who keep that physical plant running; cutting programs on health; and, cutting programs on housing.
While I will be voting with my caucus against this borrowing bill, the issue is much larger. What Canada needs is a new Constitution, not just a new back-room division of powers between a Prime Minister and a bunch of premiers, but a Constitution in which the people of Canada participate and build up strong public pressure so that the people of Canada can regain control of the government by regaining parliamentary control of the cabinet.
I see you are signalling that my time is up. I hope that there will be more occasions when these same points can be raised in this House before the government decides to gag all debate.
March 20,1991

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to voice my strong objections on behalf of my constituents in Haldimand-Norfolk to the spending priorities of this government.
My riding has been hit hard by the government's six years of economic mismanagement. Hundreds of farmers have declared bankruptcy. Hundreds of plant workers have lost their jobs. Hundreds of stores and small businesses have shut their doors. People are suffering. I say that to the member for Cariboo-Coquitlam, who is now not going to stay around to listen to this. After six years of taking money from the farmers, the storekeepers and the plant workers of Haldimand-Norfolk and giving nothing in return, frustration and anger is rampant. Cynicism with politicians is at an all time high. I feel it is incumbent upon this government to do something about that cynicism.
For six years, the people of my riding have seen this government cut their agricultural programs, cut their social programs, chop away at the mainstays of rural communities, the post offices, the railway stations and now, the community newspapers. Every year, while this government has chopped away, it has raised taxes. After six years of cutting valuable programs and raising taxes, the public debt has doubled. The deficit still continues to rise.
The government has brought our country into a recession. Canadians want to know where all the money has gone. They want to know why needy Canadians, middle-class Canadians, unemployed Canadians, farmers, fishermen, plant workers, and small entrepreneurs are always the first ones to be taxed and the last ones to be served by this government.
The Minister of Finance likes to paint himself as the sole, lone voice of fiscal sanity, a preacher of fiscal restraint. It is on the basis of these preachings that all criticisms are dismissed as irresponsible, fiscally naive. The problem is that these preachings are little more than self-serving and empty rhetoric, designed to obscure the fact that the government has fumbled its chance of bringing down the deficit and that it has made some major economic miscalculations, which have put many Canadians, including Canadians in my riding, in dire straits. Now the government is asking Canadians to bite a few more bullets.
Government Orders
The fact of the matter is that this government has squandered the public's trust. It has squandered Canadian tax dollars. The Canadian people do not believe the government any more. It is going to make it more difficult for us as politicians to come up with solutions to this fiscal mismanagement and this mess.
This government has very little credibility left. Last year, for instance, the Minister of Finance said that the deficit would fall below $28.5 billion in 1990. In fact it rose to $30.5 billion. Last year the Minister of Finance said that personal income taxes would rise by 9 per cent from the year earlier. Now he says that they will have to be raised by 15 per cent. Last year the Minister of Finance said that corporate income taxes would fall by 2 per cent. Do you know what they will fall by now, Mr. Speaker? It will be 10 per cent.
I do not think that is fair and I do not think Canadians believe that is fair. Unfortunately they do not feel they have a way of telling this government-or they do not have a way of making this government listen-that these things are not fair.
Last year again the Minister of Finance said the economy would grow by 3 per cent. He now says he thinks it will shrink by 1 per cent: 1, 2, 3 per cent. He is not sure. Last year he said employment would grow by 1.2 per cent. Now he says it will actually shrink by 1.5 per cent.
The facts speak for themselves. The Minister of Finance has no credibility. The things I have pointed out show that his credibility is seriously lacking not only in the House, not only with ordinary Canadians across the country, but also with the business community, those so-called people whom he represents, his Bay Street buddies.
This year's spending estimates signal to Canadians that this government has still not learned from its past errors. This government seems to be prepared to mismanage and fumble its way through yet another year and bring yet another year of unnecessary financial hardship all across this country, as each of us has heard in the House and in our constituency offices. On a weekly basis I heard from farmers who have lost their farms and from small businesses that have put enormous amounts of effort, time and money into providing a business and into trying to provide a future for their children. They come to my office in tears because they feel that they have been wronged by this government. They feel that had they just been left alone to their own avails they could have survived, they could have got through this recession.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
Because of this government's economic policies they feel they have just not been treated right.
Thming to tobacco farmers, once again this year they were hit hardest by this government's budget, by this government's taxation on tobacco products. This year's budget brought yet another massive tax increase on tobacco products so that an additional $1.5 billion could be pumped into the government's coffers.
It was a tax grab. The finance minister unfortunately knew that if he did not do it the Ontario NDP government would have done the same thing. Every year it seems to be a fight to see who can first put out their budget, who can first tax tobacco products and hurt the tobacco farmers who produce those products.
Not many people across this country realize that tobacco brings in close to $6 billion annually into the coffers of government. Where does that money come from? Unfortunately that is a question this government and the Minister of Finance are not prepared to even look at. He did not have the courtesy before he brought down this budget to have a meeting with the tobacco board, to have a meeting with tobacco farmers, or to have a meeting with the communities affected by tobacco, to see how such an increase in tobacco taxes would affect them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on the borrowing bill as it gives me an opportunity to make my comments on the government's recent budget, not having had an opportunity to do so before the vote on the amendment. There are two days remaining in the budget debate, but given the attitude of the government it seems unlikely that we will have those for some period of time.
I can understand its reluctance to discuss this particular disaster.
When I was considering my remarks this evening, I had a look at some old magazines, and I pulled out the Maclean's magazine for January 7, 1985, which had this headline on its front cover: "A Confident Nation Speaks Up". The magazine ran a story about polls that had been conducted by some friends of the government, Decima Research.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: I didn't know we had any.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The hon. member says:"I didn't know we had any". Well he does not have many left now, but this was in 1985. He may recall that in 1984 his party won a very substantial majority, to the great chagrin of Canadians today. The first paragraph of this article says:
Treading water is no longer our national sport. Instead of cringing before uncertain economic indicators, shaking fists at politicians or bowing to hidebound social restraints, most Canadians at mid-decade are confident about themselves and optimistic about their country.
That is what Peter C. Newman wrote in an essay based on the Decima poll conducted by Maclean's magazine in December 1984 and published in January 1985.
Then I took out the January 1, 1990 edition of Maclean's magazine, six years of Conservative government mismanagement. It said: "An Uncertain Nation, Canada at a Crossroads". That was on January 1.
On January 7, it said: "A Shaken Nation Bares its Anger." These are all based on the same poll done by Decima research obviously in late 1990. Six years of disastrous government have brought Canadians to their knees begging this government to get out so we can get a proper government that can administer the affairs of this country in a way that will give Canadians confidence in their future and optimism that the whole place is not falling apart as a result of the policies of this government.
Let me read the quote from the January 7 issue of Maclean's. This is describing the Decima poll:
The poll paints an unsettling portrait of a nation that has lost its way. English-Canadians have only grudging tolerance for continued negotiations over the status of Quebec. As they lose respect for their politicians, people are demanding more personal influence over critical decisions-with a significant 27 per cent flirting with the idea of eliminating government altogether. As well, large numbers of respondents, alienated by the size of their tax bills, want to restrict government's ability to spend. They are less optimistic than ever before in the history of the Maclean's!Decima poll about their own, and the country's, economic prospects. And on a personal level, many of them say that they feel unsafe on the streets of their communities-or even in their own homes. Said by veteran pollster, Allan Gregg, president of Toronto-based Decima Research Limited, which conducts the poll: "Certainly, in the seven years that we have been doing this research, we have never identified a blacker mood."
Allan Gregg is no friend of the Liberal Party. He is in on all the Conservative Party conferences. I am sure that all the hon. members opposite have seen him at meetings that their party has had. He is considered their principal adviser on polls. Here he is saying that Canadians are in the blackest mood they have ever found in the polling that they have done.
March 20, 1991

I say it is the direct result of the disastrous policies pursued by the hon. gentlemen opposite.
I would like to go back again in history to a budget speech delivered in this House on March 23, 1985. We know it was the present Minister of Finance who was finance minister in 1985 who did it. Let me read part of another wonderful quote from the hon. minister's speech of May 23, 1985:
I am implementing a clear and realistic medium-term plan to control our debt. That plan requires tough actions to be taken now. There will be expenditure reductions and tax increases. The impact of these actions, and those taken in November, will continue to grow. Our actions will directly reduce the annual deficit at the end of the decade by more than $20 billion. Between now and then, our actions will cut a total of $75 billion from the projected increase in the public debt.
I do not know where the Minister of Finance got his figures. I will bet it was from a crystal ball. It ceased to function, because the end of the decade was 1990. That was the end of the decade in which he was speaking, and the deficit in the financial year ended March 31, 1986 which was the year in which this budget was delivered was exactly the same as it is today. Exactly the same.
In other words, the minister defrauded Canadians in March 1985 with his statistics and his figures. He did not keep his promise to reduce government expenditure. He increased taxes. He has increased them 32 times since he took office, and a whole bunch of them were in this budget in 1985.
Government expenditure has continued to increase throughout the period, and the deficit has stayed at $30 billion. It has not gone down. It has gone up for the last three years. That is the record of financial incompetence on the part of the minister that has caused Canadians to lose confidence in their government and their governmental institutions in this country.
Mr. Speaker, in case you think I am being unfairly critical with the minister, let's look at the information that he gets. We all know that the Minister of Finance, in the course of preparation of his budget, consults with various groups across the country. He is sent free advice. He gets it from the Economic Council of Canada, from business and labour groups and, I presume, the minister listens to these groups in the course of his discussions.
Government Orders
I have here the pre-budget submission to the Minister of Finance prepared in December 1990 by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. I apologize for the extensive quotations tonight, but I could not put the words better myself. I should say that the Canadian Federation of Independent Business is not a particular friend of the Liberal Party. It has got, I am sure, more Conservatives than Liberals in it, but listen to what they say about the Minister of Finance and his inability to manage the affairs of this country. I will read from the introduction of their pre-budget submission.
The Canadian small and medium-sized business community is currently saddled with the greatest number of negative factors affecting their business that they have faced in some time. Even in the recession of 1981-82, the outlook was not as consistently negative as it is today.

speechtext: I dispute that.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The hon. member says he disputes it. He should have met with the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and disputed it. This is the submission they gave to his minister and his minister knows that this is exactly correct.
It then goes on:
However, all Canadians are now having to pay for this government mismanagement.
There is no doubt that action on government overspending may soon be forthcoming, but it will be forced upon, as opposed to chosen by, a bankrupt government. Since the government squandered the opportunities available through the mid-to late-1980s to get its spending under control in an environment of economic expansion, it will now be forced to cut back at the worst possible time-in the middle of a serious recession. And even worse, the introduction of a major new tax, the Goods and Services Thx, will only exacerbate the problems for small and medium-sized companies. Although the GST as proposed is rife with structural and design flaws, perhaps its most daunting long-term implication is that with such a money machine in place, any incentive that may currently exist for government to contain its spending will be gone. For all of these reasons, the 1984 to 1990 period can truly be described as six wasted years.
I suggest to you that they were worse than wasted. The government has damaged Canadian confidence in themselves. It has weakened their confidence in their country. It has been more than a waste, it has been a disaster.
The other point that is made in this report, I could go on reading.
When the current federal government assumed power in 1984, the small and medium-sized business community was willing to give the benefit of the doubt to the election platform promise of improved fiscal management, and believed that small firms would at least be given a fair hearing. It is now apparent to small business owners that they have been disappointed on both counts. As a result of fiscal and
