monetary policies that have been at odds for several years, but notably over the past 18 months, small firms now face the deadly combination of very high interest rates and a burgeoning federal debt. Adding these unfortunate circumstances to an inevitable slowdown in an economy after seven years of economic expansion, and the result is a self-imposed recession, that will be deepened and prolonged by government policy.
For weeks and weeks in this House, we have been asserting this fact that the policy of the government has contributed to the recession and has deepened and made it worse for Canadians.
The one other point I think that is worth mentioning in this report, and I could go on at great length on this, unfortunately my time is limited, is the gap between Canadian and U.S. interest rates. The report says of them that although these rates did not widen in 1981-82 although rates in both countries rose, this gap has been persistently in excess of 4 percentage points for some time.
The devastating impact of such an interest rate differential, and its role in maintaining the Canadian dollar at an uncompetitively high level, has been demonstrated in the recent spate of layoffs, plant closings, bankruptcies, the migration of Canadian firms to more competitive environments in the U.S. and elsewhere, and in the increased competitive pressure Canadian firms are experiencing from foreign firms from their own domestic markets.
The hon. member for Etobicoke North has asked questions regularly in this House on this subject demanding to know why the Minister of Finance will not stop his crazy interest rate policy, why he will not tell the Bank of Canada Governor to stop paying himself and his employees substantial increases and get the interest rate down, take a penalty instead of a bonus for their incompetence in managing this aspect of our policy and see that we get the differential and the rates down between Canada and the United States to increase our competitive position.
Unfortunately his pleas fall on deaf ears. The Minister of Finance gives facile answers and we get nowhere.
The other aspect of the budget that I think is extremely important is the cuts that the government announced to the provinces in respect of medicare and education. Clearly, they have put our medical care system at risk. Clearly they have weakened the ability of our provinces to deliver in the education and medical field.
We keep hearing from the government, whenever this objection is raised, that: "No, no, we have no intention of dismantling medicare. Everything is safe and sound". Although it has not used this term recently, I suspect it is nervous, the sacred trust argument is something that medicare once was. We have not heard that expression lately, but I expect if we press the Prime Minister on it, he would say it is still a sacred trust.
Yet last night in the House we had the spectacle of the Prime Minister of Canada and every single member of the Conservative Party who was here rise in his place and vote against a motion that read as follows:
That this House reaffirm its commitment to medicare.
In other words, the Conservative Party disaffirmed its commitment to medicare last night in the House. The Conservative Party, through the government House leader, who squawked and yacked yesterday afternoon about this, said that it was not possible for him to vote for this motion because somehow it would bring the government down.
He has a very short memory. On November 24, 1989, in this House, and this government was sitting on those benches, I was sitting on this side, there was an opposition and there was a government, the same one, the government allowed to pass unanimously a motion on a supply day moved by the hon. member, as he then was, for Oshawa, Mr. Broadbent. The motion talked about aid for children, expressing its concern for children living in poverty. The government could vote for that and yet it could not support medicare. In other words, the Conservatives said: "We are prepared to write medicare off". They said it by their vote last night and we know perfectly well that their actions in the budget have purported to do exactly that.

speechtext: It is a secret agenda.

It is a secret agenda, as the hon. member for Hamilton West says.
The government has no intention of assisting the provinces in this regard. It is saying to the provinces: "Raise your own money. If you can't afford the medicare system that can be afforded in Hamilton, or Toronto or in Kingston, that's too bad". Canadians are going to end up with different standards of care across this country. This government could not give two hoots about it. That is the attitude, that is the approach. I submit it is not a good approach.
March 20, 1991

I could go on about waste too. I am tempted to do so, but let me pass on to education. The minister also received advice in respect of education. The Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada in its pre-budget submission to the Minister of Finance in December 1990 among other recommendations recommended this:
That the government commit itself to a genuine reform of the Established Programs Financing arrangements.
That, until such time as the Established Programs Financing arrangements are reformed, the federal government honour its EPF funding commitments in support of postsecondary education as they stood prior to the introduction of Bill C-69.
Not only did the government not honour the commitments that existed prior to the introduction of that much opposed bill, but it also changed the rules to reduce the payments under EPF transfers to the provinces for a period following the restriction contained in Bill C-69. That is hardly the way to enhance and improve the quality of education in Canada. I of course having a very famous university in my riding, two in fact-Queen's University and the Royal Military College-I can only point out the disastrous consequences of these cuts.
While all of these events may not have happened at Queen's, they are happening at other universities across the country, in McMaster for example in the riding of Hamilton West and I could name others. Obviously there cannot be many in Conservative ridings or they would be more concerned about this. Members on the other side would be up condemning their government for cutting these transfers.
It is stated to me, and I have every reason to believe it to be so, that first and second year science students in Canada are denied a place in the laboratory to work. They are not allowed to work in a lab because there is not sufficient laboratory space in the universities for them to work in those labs. How can one maintain an interest in science if one is denied hands-on work in a laboratory as part of your educational experience until year three on a limited basis and then in year four.
Government Orders
Class sizes have increased enormously because there is not enough money to pay for professors to be hired in the universities to do the teaching. Equipment and facilities are deteriorating in universities because they cannot be maintained on the tight budgets they are operating on. They cannot be replaced on the tight budgets they are operating on and new purchases cannot be made because there is no funding available.
In the province of Ontario, my home province, the situation unfortunately, is probably going to get worse, because not only have we got a tight-fisted Conservative Government in Ottawa, but we are saddled with the New Democratic Party government in Toronto who has done nothing to show leadership and try to offset the disastrous consequences of federal government policies launched by this government on the other side.
Indeed, we have no expectation that the situation will improve in Ontario with the government there.

Even my hon. friend from Edmonton East would acknowledge that the NDP government has been a terrible disappointment in the many months it has been in office.
At the end of my remarks I would like to say that we in the Liberal Party would have expected this year, certainly a continuation of the policy of restraint we supposedly have witnessed for six years. I say that we have not had that kind of expectation when there has been a serious recession put upon us by the government's own policies in the latter part of 1990.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Spending your way out of a recession does not work. We found that out in 1981.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: We expected the government to come up with some extra generosity. Loosen the purse strings to help Canadians who are finding themselves unemployed because of the hard-hearted policies of the government.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Is there anything good about this government?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
At a time when the government is asking Canadians to restrain themselves, it goes on spending binges and wild extravagances on little things. But they add up.

March 20, 1991
Government Orders
I just got an answer the other day to a question on the Order Paper. I put a question on the Order Paper about royal commissions. We know about the Spicer Commission and its budget of $27 million.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Is Spicer wasting money? Say it. Say national unity is a waste of money.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: The hon. member asks if Spicer is a waste of money. I say the Spicer Commission is costing millions more than it should be costing if it were properly managed. He knows it. And if he does not know it, he should go to the consumer and corporate affairs committee and hear it.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: I was there last night and I listened.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Well listen again on Thursday.
I want to talk about the other royal commissions. I know the hon. member does not want to hear this. He is embarrassed by these facts and he should be. The Royal Commission on National Passenger Transportation is projected to cost $23 million. The Royal Commission on New Reproductive Technologies, $24.7 million and the Royal Commission on Electoral Reform and Party Financing, $19.9 million. We have over $100 million committed to royal commissions in Canada, that this government has set up in order to generate business for a good number of its friends and keep the various
researchers and so on, working in Canada. I say this is not a wise or prudent expenditure of public funds. It is time the government acted the way it is preaching and tightened up the purse strings in reasonable areas, instead of cutting training programs for those who are unemployed. It is a hard-hearted way to run a government.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Resign. Resign over there.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: I suggest the Minister of Finance should be ashamed of his budget and withdraw it.
